blocks.h: (a) The mandatory requirements and the approval procedure
1. What the RO Code is, and how it binds

blocks.p: The Code for Recognized Organizations (RO Code) was adopted by the Organization by resolutions MSC.349(92) and MEPC.237(65), and took effect on 1 January 2015 upon entry into force of the corresponding amendments to the 1974 SOLAS Convention and the 1988 Load Lines Protocol. It is given mandatory force for SOLAS purposes through regulation XI-1/1. It is a single consolidated instrument: before it, the criteria for recognizing an organization were spread across Assembly resolutions and applied unevenly.

The Code's own purpose statement is that it serves as the international standard and consolidated instrument containing minimum criteria against which organizations are assessed towards recognition and authorization, and the guidelines for the oversight by flag States. Its scope paragraph records that it establishes four things, and the four map directly onto this question:

ul: the mandatory requirements an organization must fulfil to be recognized by a flag State;
the mandatory requirements an RO must fulfil when performing statutory certification and services on behalf of its authorizing flag States;
the mandatory requirements flag States shall adhere to when authorizing an RO; and
guidelines for flag State oversight of ROs.

blocks.p: Structurally the Code has three parts, and knowing which is which is worth more than any single detail in it:

rows: Part 1
General - purpose, scope, contents, delegation of authority, communication of information, references
General provisions
Part 2
Recognition and authorization requirements for organizations
MANDATORY - binds both the organization and the flag State
Part 3
Oversight of recognized organizations
RECOMMENDATORY - guidance, expressly non-mandatory

blocks.p: Two definitions govern everything that follows, and candidates who blur them cannot explain the Code's structure. Recognition is the flag State's assessment of an organization against Part 2. Authorization is the separate, later act of delegating specified statutory functions to an organization that is already recognized. An organization can be recognized and still not be authorized for a particular ship type or a particular convention.

blocks.h: 2. The power to delegate, and the limit on it

blocks.p: Part 1 section 4 is the enabling provision. A flag State may delegate authority to an organization recognized as complying with the Code, to perform on its behalf statutory certification and services under mandatory IMO instruments and its national legislation. Two limits sit immediately alongside it:

ul: The flag State shall not authorize functions beyond the RO's capabilities, and in this respect shall take appendix 2 of the Code into consideration. Capability is assessed function by function, not once and for all.
Flag States should cooperate with each other with the objective of ensuring that ROs to whom they delegate authority adhere to the Code.

blocks.p: The conventional bases for the delegation itself are collected in Part 2 section 8.1: regulation I/6 of SOLAS 1974, article 13 of Load Lines 66, regulation 6 of MARPOL Annex I, regulation 8 of MARPOL Annex II and article 6 of TONNAGE 69. Under these a flag State may authorize an RO to act on its behalf in statutory certification and services and in the determination of tonnages, only for ships entitled to fly its flag. Such authorizations shall not require ROs to perform actions that impinge on the rights of another flag State.

blocks.h: 3. Approval step one - the general requirements the organization must satisfy

blocks.p: Part 2 section 2 opens with the controlling proposition: delegation of authority by a flag State to an organization shall be subject to the confirmation of the capability of that organization to demonstrate that it has the capacity to deliver high standards of service and its compliance with the requirements of this Code and applicable national legislation. The demonstration is the organization's; the confirmation is the flag State's. The heads are:

headers: What the flag State must be satisfied of
rows: 2.2 Rules and regulations

The organization establishes, publishes and systematically maintains its own rules or regulations for the design, construction and certification of ships and their associated essential engineering systems, a version of which is provided in English, and has adequate research capability to keep the published criteria updated
2.3 Independence

Neither the RO nor its staff engages in activities that may conflict with their independence of judgement and integrity. Those carrying out the statutory work are not the designer, manufacturer, supplier, installer, purchaser, owner, user or maintainer of the item certified, nor the authorized representative of any of them. The RO shall not be substantially dependent on a single commercial enterprise for its revenue
2.4 Impartiality

Personnel are free from any pressures that might affect their judgement, and procedures prevent external persons or organizations influencing the results. All potential customers have access without undue financial or other conditions, and the procedures are administered in a non-discriminatory manner
2.5 Integrity
The RO is governed by the principles of ethical behaviour contained in a Code of Ethics, which recognizes the inherent responsibility associated with a delegation of authority
2.6 Competence
Statutory work is performed by competent surveyors and auditors, duly qualified, trained and authorized to execute all duties within their level of work responsibility
2.7 Responsibility
The RO defines and documents the responsibilities, authorities, qualifications and interrelation of personnel whose work affects the quality of its services
2.8 Transparency
Access to, or disclosure of, information relating to the statutory work carried out on the flag State's behalf

blocks.p: Independence is the head that matters most, and it is worth saying why. The structural weakness of the whole arrangement is that the body doing the surveying is paid by the owner being surveyed. The revenue-dependence rule and the prohibition on certifying what you designed, supplied or maintain are the Code's direct answer to that, and an answer that lists the seven heads without identifying which one the Code is really defending has described the requirements without understanding them.

blocks.h: 4. Approval step two - the organizational, resource and process assessment

blocks.p: Being independent and competent in principle is not enough; Part 2 then assesses how the organization actually runs. The flag State examines it against four further sections:

ul: Section 3 - Management and organization. A documented quality, safety and pollution prevention policy; documentation requirements and a quality manual; control of documents and of records; planning; the organizational structure; communication internally, with the flag State and between ROs; and management review with defined review inputs and outputs.
Section 4 - Resources. Personnel, infrastructure and work environment adequate to the tasks assigned.

Section 5 - Statutory certification and services processes. Design and development inputs, outputs, verification and change control; control of production and service provision; subcontracting and service suppliers; control of monitoring and measuring devices; and a complaints and appeals process.

Section 6 - Performance measurement, analysis and improvement. Internal audit; vertical contract audit; monitoring and measurement of processes; the control, monitoring and measurement of non-conformities including statutory deficiencies; and improvement through data analysis, corrective action and preventive action.

blocks.p: Two of these are worth naming explicitly in an answer because they are what distinguish a real assessment from a paper one. The vertical contract audit follows a single ship's certification right through the organization rather than sampling processes in isolation. And section 6.5 requires the RO to control and measure statutory deficiencies, not merely its own internal non-conformities - which is how the flag State's interest gets into the RO's own quality data.

The qualification of the people is not left general. Appendix 1 sets out requirements for the training and qualification of the RO's technical staff, including theoretical and practical training, plan approval staff, survey staff and audit staff, and the assessment and maintenance of training effectiveness. Appendix 2 specifies the survey and certification functions ROs perform on behalf of the flag State, by elementary module.

blocks.h: 5. Approval step three - certification of the quality management system

blocks.p: Part 2 section 7 is a separate step and is frequently missed. It requires two distinct things:

ul: 7.1 - the RO shall develop, implement and maintain an effective internal quality management system that complies with the Code and is based on appropriate parts of internationally recognized quality standards no less effective than the ISO 9000 series.

7.2 - that system shall be periodically assessed and certified by a qualified body, accredited by an accreditation body that is a signatory to the International Accreditation Forum Multinational Recognition Agreement, recognized by the flag State as having the necessary governance and competences to act independently of the ROs or their associations.

blocks.p: The operative word is independently. It is not enough for the RO to run a quality system, nor for the industry to certify itself; the certifying body must be accredited and independent of the ROs and their associations. Section 7.3 adds that IMO itself endeavours to closely monitor the certification and audit process of ROs and will establish the working methods and rules of procedure for that monitoring.

blocks.h: 6. Approval step four - the act of authorization, and what the flag State must specify

blocks.p: Only now does the flag State authorize. Part 2 section 8 sets out what it must do, and this is the heart of limb (a) because it is the only part of the Code that is a procedure rather than a standard.

headers: What the flag State shall do
rows: 8.2 Legal basis

Establish the legal basis under which the authorization is administered, considering: the formal written agreement with the RO; acts, regulations and supplementary information; interpretations; and deviations and equivalent solutions
8.3 Specification of authorization

Specify the scope of the authorization granted. Nine specifications shall be considered: ship types and sizes; conventions and other instruments including national legislation; approval of drawings; approval of materials and equipment; surveys, audits, inspections; issuance, endorsement and/or renewal of certificates; corrective actions; withdrawal or cancellation of certificates; and reporting requirements
8.4 Resources
Ensure the RO has adequate resources in technical, managerial and research capabilities to accomplish the tasks assigned, in accordance with the minimum standards in Part 2
8.5 Instruments

Provide the RO with access to all appropriate instruments of national law giving effect to the conventions, notify it of additions, deletions or revisions in advance of their effective date, and specify whether the flag State's standards go beyond convention requirements
8.6 Instructions

Issue specific instructions detailing the procedures for carrying out the work, and the actions to be followed if a ship is found not fit to proceed to sea without danger to the ship or persons on board or presenting an unreasonable threat of harm to the marine environment; and ensure by appropriate means that ROs cooperate with each other
8.7 Records
Specify that the RO maintains records that can provide the flag State with data to assist in the interpretation of convention regulations

blocks.p: The word to underline in limb (a) is 'specify'. A general authorization to 'act on our behalf' does not satisfy section 8.3. The scope has to be written down function by function and convention by convention, and note that it must cover the unglamorous end as well - corrective actions, and the withdrawal or cancellation of certificates. A flag State that has not specified who may withdraw a certificate has not finished authorizing.

blocks.h: 7. Approval step five - the written agreement and the notification to IMO

blocks.p: Two procedural acts complete the approval, and both are commonly omitted from answers.

The formal written agreement. Appendix 3 sets out the elements a formal written agreement or equivalent between the flag State and the RO should as a minimum cover: application; purpose; general conditions; the execution of functions under authorization (general authorization, special or additional authorization, the relationship between the organization's statutory and other related activities, and functions to cooperate with port States to facilitate rectification of reported port State control deficiencies); the legal basis of those functions (acts and regulations, interpretations, deviations and equivalent solutions); reporting to the flag State; development of rules and regulations and the exchange of information; and other conditions.

The notification to IMO. Part 1 section 5 requires the flag State to communicate to, and deposit with, the Secretary-General of IMO a list of its ROs, for circulation to interested parties for the information of their officers, together with a notification of the specific responsibilities and conditions of the authority delegated. This is what makes a port State able to know, before it inspects, exactly what the certificate in front of it represents.

blocks.h: (b) The oversight mechanisms in the RO Code
8. What oversight is, and the status of Part 3

blocks.p: Part 3 of the RO Code provides guidance on flag State's oversight of ROs authorized to perform statutory certification and services on its behalf, and on the principles of oversight, which may include ship inspection, auditing and monitoring activities. Its scope paragraph is explicit that Part 3 provides guidance, which is non-mandatory, to assist flag States in developing and implementing an effective oversight programme. The adopting resolution reinforces this: it recommends Governments to use the recommendatory provisions of part 3 as a basis for relevant standards, unless their national requirements provide at least an equivalent degree of safety.

Saying this is a mark, not a hedge. It explains why Part 3 says should throughout where Part 2 says shall, and it is the reason flag States' oversight programmes differ in form while converging in substance.

Part 3 section 4 supplies the vocabulary the rest of it uses - audit (a systematic, independent and documented process for obtaining audit evidence and evaluating it objectively against audit criteria), audit criteria, audit evidence, and audit findings, which the Code notes can indicate conformity, observation (potential non-conformity), non-conformity, or opportunities for improvement.

blocks.h: 9. Mechanism one - supervision of the delegated duties

blocks.p: Part 3 section 5.2 sets out what the flag State's supervision of duties delegated to an RO should consider, inter alia:

ol: documentation of the RO's quality management system;
access to the RO's internal instructions, circulars and guidelines;
access to the RO's documentation relevant to the flag State's fleet;
cooperation with the flag State's inspection and verification work; and
provision of information and statistics, such as but not limited to damage and casualties relevant to the flag State's fleet.

blocks.p: The thread running through all five is access. Oversight is impossible if the flag State can see only the certificates the RO chose to issue, so the Code puts the RO's internal instructions and its fleet documentation within the flag State's reach as a matter of course.

blocks.h: 10. Mechanism two - verification and monitoring, and the RO's reporting duties

blocks.p: Part 3 section 5.3 requires the flag State to establish a system to ensure the adequacy of statutory certification and services provided. That system should include procedures for communication with the RO, procedures for reporting by the RO and the processing of those reports, additional ship inspections by the flag State, technical and safety consultations between ROs where certificate validity may be affected, the flag State's evaluation and acceptance of the RO's QMS certification by an independent body of auditors, and monitoring and verification of the statutory work itself.
The reporting requirements are the most concrete thing in Part 3 and should be given as a list:

rows: A major deficiency or serious safety-related issue that would normally be considered sufficient to detain a ship from proceeding to sea pending correction
Notify the flag State
Immediately on becoming aware
A major non-conformity aboard ship or within a company, as defined in the Guidelines on the Implementation of the ISM Code by Administrations
Notify the flag State(s)
Immediately on becoming aware
Either of the above
The notification contains the name of the company or ship, the IMO number, the official number if applicable, and a description of the non-conformity, deficiency or issue
With the notification
Dangerous occurrences, accidents, machinery or structural breakdowns or failures on a ship
Inform the flag State
As soon as possible
Removal of a ship from the RO's list of classed or certified ships for which it performed statutory work
Report to the flag State in writing, with names, official numbers if applicable and the reasons for removal from class
Within 30 days of the removal becoming effective

blocks.p: The monitoring and verification limb at 5.3 also identifies what the flag State should consider implementing: oversight of the RO's quality management systems; observation of, or systematic review of the reports of, QMS audits conducted by qualified persons or organizations external to and independent of the RO; verification and inspection of ships subject to statutory certification; and a complaint and feedback system with corrective action follow-up. Two further items close a real gap: a flag State accepting ships constructed without its involvement should establish that the RO conducting their statutory work conforms to the Code, and for ships built without an identified flag State, flag-specific requirements should be verified before certification.

blocks.h: 11. Mechanism three - auditing

blocks.p: Part 3 section 6 is short and worth knowing precisely. The flag State should be satisfied that the RO has an effective quality management system in place, and may rely upon the audits carried out by an accredited certification body or equivalent organizations; intergovernmental cooperation in establishing common auditing practices is encouraged. A flag State auditor should advance three principles:

ul: Ethical conduct - the foundation of professionalism; trust, integrity, confidentiality and discretion are essential to auditing.

Fair presentation - the obligation to report truthfully and accurately, so that findings, conclusions and reports reflect the audit activities, with significant obstacles encountered and unresolved diverging opinions between the audit team and the auditee reported.
Due professional care - the application of diligence and judgement, in accordance with the importance of the task and the confidence placed in the auditor.

blocks.p: The permission to rely on third-party audits is the practical heart of this section: it is what makes oversight affordable for a flag State that cannot audit every RO itself, and it is also the reason section 7 requires the certifying body to be accredited and independent.

blocks.h: 12. Mechanism four - managing the oversight programme

blocks.p: Part 3 section 7 turns the individual activities into a managed programme, and the structure is worth reproducing because it is what 'programme' means:

ul: 7.2 Objectives and extent - the objectives of the programme, and its extent, which should reflect the size, nature and complexity of the flag State's authorization programme, the scope, objective and duration of monitoring activities, the frequency of monitoring, the number, importance, complexity, similarity and locations of the ROs, applicable standards and contractual requirements, the need for accreditation or registration, and the conclusions of previous monitoring.

7.3 Responsibilities, resources and procedures - who owns the programme; the financial resources to develop, implement, manage and improve it; auditing techniques; processes to achieve and maintain the competence of staff; the availability of staff and technical experts; documented procedures; implementation; and programme records.
7.4 Monitoring and reviewing - the programme is itself monitored to confirm its objectives are being met, and reviewed periodically.

blocks.p: Note that the flag State's own additional ship inspections sit inside this programme rather than beside it. Inspecting a sample of the RO's ships is not a substitute for oversight; it is one of the programme's monitoring activities and it is planned as such.

blocks.h: 13. Mechanism five - the performance indicators

blocks.p: The printed stem asks about continued compliance and performance. Part 3 section 7.4.3 is the performance half, and it gives the flag State five indicators to consider when evaluating the performance of ROs:

ol: port State performance of ROs;
results of the RO's internal audits;
results of quality management system audits performed by third-party organizations;
the results of previous performance monitoring; and
condition and compliance of the ships that receive survey and certification from the ROs.

blocks.p: The Code also turns the mirror on the flag State itself. Section 7.4.4 requires the flag State to evaluate periodically its own performance in implementing the administrative processes, procedures and resources necessary to meet its convention obligations, and 7.4.5 lists measures for doing so, including port State control detention rates, flag State inspection results, casualty statistics, communication and information processes and annual loss statistics excluding constructive total losses, together with further indicators such as fleet loss and accident ratios, detained ships in relation to fleet size, verified cases of incompetence or wrongdoing by certificate holders, responses to port State deficiency reports, investigations into very serious and serious casualties and the lessons learned from them, and the results of inspections, surveys and controls of the fleet.

That last item is the connection worth making in an exam: the same casualty investigations that flow from SOLAS regulation XI-1/6 feed back into how the flag State judges its own performance and its ROs'. Oversight is not a closed administrative loop.

blocks.h: 14. What follows a finding, and why the scheme exists at all

blocks.p: Where oversight identifies a shortfall, the flag State's options run along the authorization it granted. Because the authorization was specified under section 8.3, it can be narrowed - by ship type, by convention, by function - as readily as it can be withdrawn, and corrective action can be required under the agreement made under appendix 3. Because the RO's obligations are conditions of the authorization and not courtesies, failure to report a detainable deficiency or a removal from class is itself a compliance failure and not merely poor service.

The closing proposition is the one to end on. The flag State may delegate the work; it cannot delegate the responsibility. The certificates carry the flag State's name, the obligation to the other Contracting Governments remains the flag State's, and the whole of Part 3 exists because an assessment made on the day of appointment says nothing about the state of the organization five years later. Approval under Part 2 and oversight under Part 3 are two halves of one duty, and the Code is built that way on purpose.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: The examiner has written the two limbs to match the two mandatory-and-recommendatory halves of the Code, and the single most valuable thing you can do in the first thirty seconds is recognise that: limb (a) is Part 2, limb (b) is Part 3. Once you have that, the answer plans itself and you will not drift into port State control, the III Code or the Member State Audit Scheme - all of which are real, all of which are about flag performance, and none of which is in the RO Code. The stem says 'outlined in the RO code' and it means it.

Limb (a) says 'requirements and procedures'. Most candidates answer the requirements and forget the procedures, and it costs them half the limb. Write it as a numbered sequence - instrument, power to delegate, three assessment steps, the authorization act, the agreement and the IMO notification - and the procedural marks arrive automatically. Limb (b) says 'mechanisms', plural, so give five and number them. A limb (b) that says 'the flag State audits the RO and monitors performance' has named one and a half of five.

The two details most likely to separate a good answer from an average one are the revenue-dependence rule in section 2.3 and the thirty-day report on removal from class in section 5.3. Both are specific, both are quotable, and both show you have read the Code rather than reasoned about what it probably says.

blocks.h: The idea underneath the Code

blocks.p: Every flag State makes the same promise under SOLAS, Load Lines, MARPOL and Tonnage: the ships on its register meet the international standard. Almost no flag State can keep that promise unaided. The classification societies already had the surveyors, the rules, the research departments and the offices in every major port, so the statutory work went to them, and it has gone to them for over a century.

The arrangement has one structural flaw that no amount of good faith removes: the surveyor's fee is paid by the party being surveyed, and the party whose name is on the certificate is often thousands of miles away and has never seen the ship. If the RO is too gentle, the flag State's promise is worthless. If the RO is commercially dependent on one owner, its judgement is not free even if its people are honest. If nobody checks the RO after appointment, an organization that was excellent in 2015 can be inadequate in 2024 and the flag State will not know.

The RO Code addresses all three. It requires structural independence, not merely declared impartiality - which is why the revenue rule exists. It requires an externally certified quality system, so that the assurance does not come from the RO's own opinion of itself. And it builds continuing oversight into the arrangement, so that recognition is a state that must be maintained rather than a status once conferred. Read that way, every section of Part 2 and Part 3 is answering one of those three problems, and the Code stops being a list to memorise.

blocks.h: Recognition, authorization and oversight - the three acts

rows: Recognition
Part 2 sections 2 to 7
Is this organization the kind of body that may hold delegated authority at all? Independent, impartial, competent, resourced, with a certified quality system
Not permission to do anything in particular
Authorization
Part 2 section 8, with appendix 3

Not a general power of attorney - the scope must be specified

blocks.p: If you can hold this table in your head you can reconstruct most of the answer under pressure, because every provision in the Code belongs to exactly one of these three columns.

blocks.h: The parts of Part 2 that candidates skip, and why they carry marks

ul: Section 5.9, subcontracting and service suppliers. An RO that subcontracts thickness measurement or radiographic testing has not thereby escaped the Code, and the flag State's assessment reaches the subcontracting controls.

Section 5.11 and 5.12, complaints and appeals. An owner who believes a surveyor has been arbitrary must have a route that is not simply 'change class'. Their presence tells you the Code treats the RO as exercising public authority, not merely selling a service.

Section 6.3, the vertical contract audit. A horizontal audit samples processes; a vertical contract audit follows one ship's certification through every process that touched it. It is the audit type that finds the failure a process audit misses.

Section 6.5, non-conformities including statutory deficiencies. The RO must measure and control the deficiencies found on the ships it certified, not only the faults in its own procedures. This is the provision that makes the RO's quality data useful to the flag State.

Section 8.5, instruments. The flag State must tell the RO in advance when national law changes and must say whether its standards go beyond convention requirements. An RO cannot enforce a national requirement it was never told about, and a flag State that has not said so cannot complain that it was not enforced.

blocks.h: How Part 3 hangs together

blocks.p: Read Part 3 as answering four questions in order. What can we see? - section 5.2, the five access items. What must they tell us, and when? - section 5.3, the reporting triggers, with the thirty-day rule as the only hard interval. How do we test it? - section 6, auditing, with permission to rely on accredited third-party audits and three principles for the flag State's own auditors. How do we run this as a programme rather than as a series of visits? - section 7, with objectives, extent, responsibilities, resources, procedures, records, review, and the five performance indicators at 7.4.3.

The elegance of section 7.4.3 is that four of the five indicators are things the flag State does not have to generate itself: port State performance comes from the MOU regimes, internal audit results and third-party QMS audit results come from the RO and its certifier, and previous performance monitoring is its own history. Only the fifth - the condition and compliance of the ships - requires the flag State to go and look. That is a deliberate design: it makes an effective oversight programme achievable for an administration with modest resources, which is precisely the administration most likely to have delegated everything.

blocks.h: The evidence position on this question, stated plainly

blocks.p: The corpus copy of the RO Code is a 61-page scan with no text layer at all - a text extraction returns zero characters. It would have been legitimate to treat this question as the paper's weakest and answer it at policy level. That is not what was done. The pages were rendered and read at source this session, which is the same read-back method MIW requires for verifying any source, and the section structure, the section numbers and the substance in this answer are taken from that reading.

Two limits remain and are stated in the answer object rather than hidden. First, the held copy is the base Code as adopted by MSC.349(92) and MEPC.237(65); no amendment is held and none is asserted in either direction, because a copy that predates an amendment cannot prove the amendment does not exist. Second, nothing is quoted from a page that was not read. If you are revising from this answer, the section numbers are reliable; the correct posture on RO Code amendments is that MIW has not established the position, not that there have been none.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: Answering limb (b) with port State control. The commonest error. PSC is a port State mechanism; the stem asks for flag State oversight mechanisms in the RO Code. PSC appears legitimately only where the Code itself uses it - as a performance indicator at 7.4.3.1 and in the appendix 3 requirement that the RO cooperate with port States to rectify reported deficiencies.
Treating recognition and authorization as one act. If they were one act, Part 2 section 8 would not exist. Say that the scope must be specified and give two or three of the nine specifications.

Saying Part 3 is mandatory. It is not, and its own scope paragraph says so. But do not overcorrect into saying it does not matter: the adopting resolution recommends it as the basis for national standards unless national requirements are at least equivalent.
Inventing an amendment. Do not attribute a date or a resolution number to an RO Code amendment. If you do not know, describe the Code as adopted and effective 1 January 2015 and move on.

Naming a class society as an example and then describing IACS. The stem is about the RO Code. IACS is a trade association of classification societies and is not a party to any authorization; its quality scheme appears in the Code only as one of the referenced documents.

Forgetting the IMO notification. The list of ROs deposited with the Secretary-General, together with the specific responsibilities and conditions of the delegated authority, is a mandatory procedural step and is a cheap mark for anyone who remembers it.

blocks.h: If you only have ten minutes for this question

blocks.p: Write eight lines for limb (a) and eight for limb (b). Limb (a): the Code and its three parts, with Part 2 mandatory and Part 3 recommendatory; the flag State may delegate but not beyond the RO's capabilities; the organization is assessed against the general requirements - independence, impartiality, integrity, competence, responsibility, transparency, published rules; its management, resources, processes and performance measurement are assessed; its quality system must be certified by an independent accredited body; the flag State then authorizes and specifies the scope, the legal basis, the instruments, the instructions and the records; a formal written agreement is concluded; and the list of ROs and the conditions of delegation are deposited with the IMO Secretary-General.

Limb (b): Part 3 is guidance; the flag State supervises the delegated duties through five access items; it establishes a verification and monitoring system under which the RO reports detainable deficiencies and major non-conformities immediately and removals from class within thirty days; it audits, or relies on accredited third-party audits, applying ethical conduct, fair presentation and due professional care; it runs this as a managed programme with objectives, extent, resources, procedures, records and review; and it evaluates RO performance against five indicators - port State performance, RO internal audits, third-party QMS audits, previous monitoring, and the condition of the certified ships. Close with the one sentence that ties both limbs together: the flag State can delegate the work but not the responsibility.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

blocks.p: These are the places this particular question goes wrong, taken from the ambiguities identified before drafting and from the single error most likely to cost marks.

The one that costs most: Answering limb (b) with port State control, the III Code or the IMO Member State Audit Scheme. Those are real mechanisms and none of them is IN THE RO CODE, which is what the stem asked for. The second trap is treating recognition and authorization as one act - they are two, and section 8 exists precisely because an organization can be recognized as competent in general and still not be authorized for a particular ship type or convention.
The wording of the stem invites four specific misreadings, and each is resolved in the answer rather than left to chance:

ul: 'Approve' is not the Code's word. The Code distinguishes RECOGNITION - assessing an organization against Part 2 - from AUTHORIZATION, the delegation of specified functions to an already recognized organization. The answer uses the Code's two words and says why the distinction matters, because a candidate who treats approval as a single act cannot explain why section 8 exists separately from section 2.

'Mandatory requirements' could be read as the requirements on the RO only. Part 2 binds BOTH: scope 2.2 records mandatory requirements for the organization to be recognized, mandatory requirements for the RO when performing services, and mandatory requirements that FLAG STATES shall adhere to when authorizing. The answer says so, because limb (a) asks what the flag State must do.

'Oversight mechanisms outlined in the RO code' is a restriction, not a topic. Port State control, the III Code and the IMO Member State Audit Scheme are all real flag-performance mechanisms and none of them is in the RO Code. They are not written, because the examiner named the instrument.

The Code's own scope paragraph 2.2.1 refers to the mandatory requirements for recognition as being in 'part 1' where the structure places them in part 2. The answer follows the STRUCTURE, which is unambiguous from the Contents and from part 2's own heading, and does not reproduce the cross-reference.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

blocks.p: The retrieval questions below are the ones this answer is built to survive. They are the same questions an examiner reaches for when testing whether a written answer was understood or reproduced.

ul: Give the route for the RO Code approval and oversight question. — 8 + 8. Limb (a) is a procedure and must read as a sequence; limb (b) is five countable mechanisms, and candidates who name only auditing lose most of the limb.

RO Code: recognition or authorization - what is the difference? — The single most common structural error on this question. An organization can be recognized and still not be authorized for a given ship type or convention.

Which parts of the RO Code are mandatory, and what did the adopting resolution say about the rest? — Limb (b) asks for the mechanisms 'outlined in the RO code'. Saying that Part 3 is guidance is a mark, not a hedge - it is the reason the Code says 'should' where Part 2 says 'shall'.
The five items in the flag State's supervision of duties delegated to an RO. — A countable list in a limb that most candidates answer in generalities.

The five performance indicators the flag State should use to evaluate an RO. — 'Continued compliance AND PERFORMANCE' is in the printed stem. This list is the performance half and it is where the discriminating marks are.
What must the RO report to the flag State, and how quickly? — The thirty-day rule is the only hard interval in Part 3 and it is the most quotable thing in limb (b).

Why does the RO Code care so much about independence and revenue? — This is the structural weakness the whole Code exists to control - the surveyor is paid by the surveyed - and naming the revenue-dependence rule shows you understand why.

What must a formal written agreement between the flag State and the RO cover? — The stem asks for PROCEDURES. The agreement is the procedural instrument that turns an assessment into an authorization, and appendix 3 is the checkable answer.

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: The route, chunked: Limb (a) is a PROCEDURE: WHAT (1), MAY (2), then three tests - WHO they are (3), HOW they run (4), WHO CHECKS THEM (5) - then AUTHORIZE (6) and SIGN AND TELL IMO (7). Limb (b) is FIVE MECHANISMS: SUPERVISE (9), VERIFY AND REPORT (10), AUDIT (11), MANAGE (12), MEASURE (13) - bracketed by STATUS (8) and CONSEQUENCE (14).

Fifteen-second recall: RO Code: MSC.349(92) + MEPC.237(65), effective 1 Jan 2015, mandatory via SOLAS XI-1/1. Part 1 general, Part 2 MANDATORY (recognition + authorization), Part 3 RECOMMENDATORY (oversight). Approve = recognize against Part 2 sections 2-7, then authorize under section 8 specifying scope, then written agreement (appendix 3) and notify IMO (Part 1 section 5). Oversee = supervise (5.2), verify and monitor with RO reporting (5.3), audit (6), manage the programme (7), measure against five performance indicators (7.4.3).

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Two limbs of eight marks each, and they are two halves of one lifecycle. Limb (a) is the FRONT END - the mandatory requirements and the PROCEDURES a flag State must follow to APPROVE an RO. The word 'procedures' is doing real work: the examiner wants a sequence, not a list of adjectives about what a good RO looks like. Limb (b) is the BACK END - the OVERSIGHT MECHANISMS OUTLINED IN THE RO CODE for CONTINUED compliance and performance. 'Outlined in the RO Code' is a deliberate restriction: the answer must give the Code's own Part 3 machinery, not a generic account of flag State control. The two limbs map exactly onto Part 2 and Part 3 of the Code, which is the single most useful thing a candidate can know before writing.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 8 + 8, printed against each limb. In limb (a), roughly one mark for what the Code is and where the power to delegate comes from, three for the substantive requirements the organization must satisfy - general requirements, organization and resources, QMS certification - three for the authorization act and what must be specified in it, and one for the agreement and the IMO notification. In limb (b), roughly two marks for supervision of the delegated duties, two for verification, monitoring and the RO's reporting duties, two for auditing and the management of the programme, and two for the performance indicators and what follows a finding. A candidate who writes limb (b) as 'the flag State audits the RO' and stops has answered one of five mechanisms.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That the candidate knows the RO Code exists as a named instrument, knows it has three parts and which of them are mandatory, and can convert that structure into an approval sequence and an oversight programme. Specifically: that recognition and authorization are two different acts; that Part 2 binds both the RO and the flag State; that Part 3 is guidance and non-mandatory but is what an examiner means by 'oversight mechanisms outlined in the RO code'; that the RO's quality management system must be certified by an independent accredited body and not merely operated; that the authorization must SPECIFY ITS SCOPE rather than being general; and that a formal written agreement and a notification to IMO are part of the procedure and not administrative afterthoughts.

Read the adopting resolution's operative paragraphs for the effective date and for the status of Part 3
Read the Contents pages in full, so the section structure quoted in the answer is the Code's own and not reconstructed

Read Part 3 sections 1 to 6 and 7.4 for the oversight programme, the reporting duties and the performance indicators
Read appendix 3 for the elements of the written agreement
Assert NO amendment to the Code, because the held copy is the base text and would not contain one

The 1 July 2024 SOLAS boundary is engaged only in the sense that SOLAS regulation XI-1/1 is cited from the Consolidated Edition 2024; MSC.521(106) introduced chapter XV and the IP Code and does not amend chapter XI-1, so the substance is unaffected and only the edition cited changes.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: MEDIUM. The question is about a flag State function that India performs through DG Shipping, and it invites an Indian statutory limb the stem does not ask for. technical_ambiguities: 'Approve' is not the Code's word. The Code distinguishes RECOGNITION - assessing an organization against Part 2 - from AUTHORIZATION, the delegation of specified functions to an already recognized organization. The answer uses the Code's two words and says why the distinction matters, because a candidate who treats approval as a single act cannot explain why section 8 exists separately from section 2.

'Mandatory requirements' could be read as the requirements on the RO only. Part 2 binds BOTH: scope 2.2 records mandatory requirements for the organization to be recognized, mandatory requirements for the RO when performing services, and mandatory requirements that FLAG STATES shall adhere to when authorizing. The answer says so, because limb (a) asks what the flag State must do.

'Oversight mechanisms outlined in the RO code' is a restriction, not a topic. Port State control, the III Code and the IMO Member State Audit Scheme are all real flag-performance mechanisms and none of them is in the RO Code. They are not written, because the examiner named the instrument.

The Code's own scope paragraph 2.2.1 refers to the mandatory requirements for recognition as being in 'part 1' where the structure places them in part 2. The answer follows the STRUCTURE, which is unambiguous from the Contents and from part 2's own heading, and does not reproduce the cross-reference.

questions.understand_first: A flag State has promised the world that the ships flying its flag are built and maintained to an international standard, and that promise is kept by surveying them. Most flag States cannot survey their own fleet - they have neither the surveyors nor the offices in the ports where their ships trade - so they hand the work to a professional body, usually a classification society, and let it issue the certificates in the flag State's name. That is a sensible arrangement with one obvious weakness: the body doing the surveying is paid by the shipowner it is surveying, and the flag State whose name is on the certificate may never see the ship. So the international answer comes in two halves. Before any work is handed over, the State must satisfy itself that the body is capable and genuinely independent, and must write down exactly which jobs it is handing over - that is the front half. And because capability on the day of appointment proves nothing about capability five years later, the State must keep watching: getting reports, auditing, inspecting some of the ships itself, and measuring how the body's ships actually perform in the world's ports - that is the back half. The Code that sets out the first half in binding terms and the second half as guidance is the RO Code, and the two halves are its Part 2 and Part 3. The idea underneath the whole thing is simple and worth holding onto: the State can delegate the work, but it cannot delegate the responsibility.
questions.memory_cue: Limb (a) is a PROCEDURE: WHAT (1), MAY (2), then three tests - WHO they are (3), HOW they run (4), WHO CHECKS THEM (5) - then AUTHORIZE (6) and SIGN AND TELL IMO (7). Limb (b) is FIVE MECHANISMS: SUPERVISE (9), VERIFY AND REPORT (10), AUDIT (11), MANAGE (12), MEASURE (13) - bracketed by STATUS (8) and CONSEQUENCE (14).

quick_revision.recall_15s: RO Code: MSC.349(92) + MEPC.237(65), effective 1 Jan 2015, mandatory via SOLAS XI-1/1. Part 1 general, Part 2 MANDATORY (recognition + authorization), Part 3 RECOMMENDATORY (oversight). Approve = recognize against Part 2 sections 2-7, then authorize under section 8 specifying scope, then written agreement (appendix 3) and notify IMO (Part 1 section 5). Oversee = supervise (5.2), verify and monitor with RO reporting (5.3), audit (6), manage the programme (7), measure against five performance indicators (7.4.3).
critical_numbers: RO Code adopted by resolutions MSC.349(92) and MEPC.237(65); took effect 1 January 2015
Three parts: Part 1 general, Part 2 mandatory, Part 3 recommendatory guidance on oversight
Part 2 section 2 - eight general requirements, 2.1 to 2.8
Part 2 section 8.3 - nine specifications of the scope of authorization
Part 3 section 5.2 - five items in the flag State's supervision of delegated duties
Part 3 section 5.3 - removal from the RO's list of classed/certified ships reported in writing within 30 days
Part 3 section 6.2 - three auditor principles: ethical conduct, fair presentation, due professional care
Part 3 section 7.4.3 - five performance indicators
quick_revision.critical_regulation: RO Code Part 2 (mandatory recognition and authorization requirements) and Part 3 (recommendatory oversight guidance), made mandatory through SOLAS regulation XI-1/1 and the corresponding MARPOL and 1988 Load Lines Protocol amendments.
quick_revision.major_trap: Answering limb (b) with port State control, the III Code or the IMO Member State Audit Scheme. Those are real mechanisms and none of them is IN THE RO CODE, which is what the stem asked for. The second trap is treating recognition and authorization as one act - they are two, and section 8 exists precisely because an organization can be recognized as competent in general and still not be authorized for a particular ship type or convention.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the RO Code approval and oversight question.
retrieval_cards.answer: Limb (a): 1 what the Code is. 2 the power to delegate and its limit. 3 general requirements. 4 organization and resources. 5 QMS certification. 6 the authorization act. 7 agreement and IMO notification. Limb (b): 8 status of Part 3. 9 supervision. 10 verification, monitoring and RO reporting. 11 auditing. 12 managing the programme. 13 performance indicators. 14 consequence.
retrieval_cards.why: 8 + 8. Limb (a) is a procedure and must read as a sequence; limb (b) is five countable mechanisms, and candidates who name only auditing lose most of the limb.

retrieval_cards.prompt: RO Code: recognition or authorization - what is the difference?
retrieval_cards.answer: RECOGNITION is the flag State's assessment of an organization against the mandatory requirements of Part 2 - that it is independent, impartial, competent, properly resourced and operating a certified quality management system. AUTHORIZATION is the separate act of delegating SPECIFIED statutory functions to an organization already recognized, and Part 2 section 8 requires the flag State to specify the scope: ship types and sizes, conventions and national legislation, drawing approval, material and equipment approval, surveys, certificate issuance, corrective actions, withdrawal of certificates and reporting.
retrieval_cards.why: The single most common structural error on this question. An organization can be recognized and still not be authorized for a given ship type or convention.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which parts of the RO Code are mandatory, and what did the adopting resolution say about the rest?
retrieval_cards.answer: Part 2 is mandatory - recognition and authorization requirements binding on both the organization and the flag State. Part 3, oversight of recognized organizations, is expressly non-mandatory guidance; its own scope paragraph says so, and the adopting resolution recommends Governments use the recommendatory provisions of part 3 as a basis for relevant standards unless their national requirements provide at least an equivalent degree of safety.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb (b) asks for the mechanisms 'outlined in the RO code'. Saying that Part 3 is guidance is a mark, not a hedge - it is the reason the Code says 'should' where Part 2 says 'shall'.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The five items in the flag State's supervision of duties delegated to an RO.
retrieval_cards.answer: Part 3 section 5.2: documentation of the RO's quality management system; access to internal instructions, circulars and guidelines; access to the RO's documentation relevant to the flag State's fleet; cooperation with the flag State's inspection and verification work; and provision of information and statistics such as damage and casualties relevant to the flag State's fleet.
retrieval_cards.why: A countable list in a limb that most candidates answer in generalities.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The five performance indicators the flag State should use to evaluate an RO.
retrieval_cards.answer: Part 3 section 7.4.3: port State performance of ROs; results of the RO's internal audits; results of quality management system audits performed by third-party organizations; the results of previous performance monitoring; and the condition and compliance of ships that receive survey and certification from the RO.
retrieval_cards.why: 'Continued compliance AND PERFORMANCE' is in the printed stem. This list is the performance half and it is where the discriminating marks are.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What must the RO report to the flag State, and how quickly?
retrieval_cards.answer: Part 3 section 5.3: immediately on becoming aware of a major deficiency or serious safety-related issue that would normally be considered sufficient to detain a ship; immediately on becoming aware of a major non-conformity aboard a ship or within a company; as soon as possible, any dangerous occurrence, accident, machinery or structural breakdown or failure it is aware of; and in writing within THIRTY DAYS, the names of any ships removed from the RO's list of classed or certified ships, with the reasons.
retrieval_cards.why: The thirty-day rule is the only hard interval in Part 3 and it is the most quotable thing in limb (b).

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why does the RO Code care so much about independence and revenue?
retrieval_cards.answer: Part 2 section 2.3 requires that the RO and its staff not engage in activities that may conflict with their independence of judgement and integrity, that those carrying out statutory work not be the designer, manufacturer, supplier, installer, purchaser, owner, user or maintainer of the item being certified nor the authorized representative of any of those parties, and that the RO NOT BE SUBSTANTIALLY DEPENDENT ON A SINGLE COMMERCIAL ENTERPRISE FOR ITS REVENUE. Section 2.4 adds that personnel shall be free from pressures that might affect their judgement.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the structural weakness the whole Code exists to control - the surveyor is paid by the surveyed - and naming the revenue-dependence rule shows you understand why.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What must a formal written agreement between the flag State and the RO cover?
retrieval_cards.answer: RO Code appendix 3 gives eight minimum headings: application; purpose; general conditions; the execution of functions under authorization; the legal basis of those functions; reporting to the flag State; development of rules and regulations and the exchange of information; and other conditions.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem asks for PROCEDURES. The agreement is the procedural instrument that turns an assessment into an authorization, and appendix 3 is the checkable answer.

blocks.h: (a) Primary objectives, key provisions, and how they enhance maritime security

blocks.p: A note on sources before the answer begins. MIW holds no licensed copy of the SUA Convention or of either 2005 Protocol. Every article below is therefore identified by number and by effect; nothing is quoted, and no sub-paragraph numbering below article level is asserted. That is a deliberate limit, not an omission.

blocks.h: 1. The gap in the law that the Convention was written to close

blocks.p: The Convention is unintelligible until you see what it was for. The pre-existing international crime was piracy, and piracy is defined around a particular picture: one ship attacking another, on the high seas, for private ends. Three features of that definition leave a hole large enough to sail a passenger ship through.

ul: No second ship. If those who seize the vessel are already on board - as passengers or as crew - there is no attacking vessel and the two-ship requirement fails.
Not private ends. If the motive is political rather than plunder, the conduct falls outside the definition however violent it is.
No duty on anyone. Even where the conduct was criminal under some national law, no treaty obliged the State in which the offenders surfaced either to try them or to hand them over.

blocks.p: The Achille Lauro seizure in 1985 demonstrated all three at once, and the diplomatic aftermath - in which the question of who could prosecute, and who was obliged to, had no clear answer - is what produced the Convention. The response was not to stretch piracy but to write a new instrument built on conduct rather than on the relationship between two vessels.

blocks.h: 2. The instruments and their dates

rows: SUA Convention 1988
1988, at Rome
Creates the principal offences and the State obligations
Fixed Platforms Protocol 1988
Extends the scheme to fixed platforms on the continental shelf
Protocol of 2005 to the Convention
Adds articles 3bis, 3ter and 3quater and the article 8bis boarding regime
Protocol of 2005 to the Fixed Platforms Protocol
The corresponding extension for fixed platforms

blocks.p: Note the plural. The stem writes 'its 2005 Protocol' in the singular; there are in fact two, and the one that matters here is the Protocol to the Convention. The fixed-platform companion is mentioned once for completeness and not pursued.

The 2005 Protocol operates by amending the 1988 Convention rather than standing alone, which is why the new offences carry bis, ter and quater numbering inside the original article 3 sequence. As between Parties to the Protocol, the Convention and the Protocol are read as a single instrument.

blocks.h: 3. The primary objectives

ol: To ensure that specified unlawful acts against the safety of maritime navigation are criminal offences in the law of every Party, so that the conduct is punishable wherever the offender is found rather than only where the ship happens to be registered.
To ensure that appropriate action is taken against the offenders - which in practice means removing the possibility of a safe haven, by obliging a Party either to extradite or to prosecute.

To establish a framework of international cooperation: an agreed allocation of jurisdiction, agreed procedures for custody and inquiry, extradition and mutual legal assistance, and the sharing of information through IMO.
To deter, by making it predictable that such conduct will be prosecuted somewhere, and after 2005, to prevent the use of ships as weapons or as delivery vehicles for weapons of mass destruction.

blocks.p: The Convention is therefore best described as a criminal-law and jurisdiction treaty. It imposes no construction standard, no equipment requirement and no shipboard procedure, and a candidate who describes it as though it did has misidentified the instrument.

blocks.h: 4. Where the Convention applies

blocks.p: Application is governed by article 4 and is keyed to the ship's navigation rather than to the location of the crime. In substance, the Convention applies where the ship is navigating or is scheduled to navigate into, through or from waters beyond the outer limit of the territorial sea of a single State, or the lateral limits of its territorial sea with adjacent States. Where that is not the case, the Convention nevertheless applies when the offender or alleged offender is found in the territory of a Party other than the State in whose waters the ship was navigating.

The practical effect is that the Convention reaches the internationally trading ship and does not intrude on a State's purely internal waterborne traffic. Warships, ships being used as naval auxiliaries or for customs or police purposes, and ships withdrawn from navigation or laid up, fall outside it.

blocks.h: 5. Key provisions one - the offences created in 1988

blocks.p: Article 3 is the offence-creating article. A person commits an offence if that person unlawfully and intentionally:

ol: seizes or exercises control over a ship by force or threat of force or any other form of intimidation;
performs an act of violence against a person on board a ship, if that act is likely to endanger the safe navigation of that ship;
destroys a ship or causes damage to a ship or to her cargo which is likely to endanger the safe navigation of that ship;
places or causes to be placed on a ship a device or substance which is likely to destroy that ship or cause damage to her or her cargo which endangers or is likely to endanger her safe navigation;
destroys or seriously damages maritime navigational facilities, or seriously interferes with their operation, if that is likely to endanger the safe navigation of a ship;
communicates information which he knows to be false, thereby endangering the safe navigation of a ship; or
injures or kills any person in connection with the commission or attempted commission of any of the above offences.

blocks.p: Article 3.2 extends liability to attempting any of these, to abetting such an offence or otherwise being an accomplice, and to threatening to commit certain of them where the threat is likely to endanger the ship's safe navigation.

The qualifying phrase is the key to the whole article. Most limbs are tied to conduct that is likely to endanger the safe navigation of the ship. That is what distinguishes a SUA offence from ordinary shipboard crime: a theft or an assault on board is a matter for the flag State's general criminal law, but an assault that puts the ship's navigation in danger engages the Convention and with it the whole international machinery. Say this in the exam - it is the difference between listing the offences and understanding them.

blocks.h: 6. Key provisions two - what the 2005 Protocol added

rows: Article 3bis

The ship as a weapon and as a carrier. Using a ship in a manner that causes death, serious injury or damage, or discharging from a ship any explosive, radioactive material, biological, chemical or nuclear weapon or other hazardous substance in a manner that causes or is likely to cause death, serious injury or damage - where the purpose is to intimidate a population or compel a government or international organization to do or abstain from an act. It also covers the transport of such weapons and materials, of certain dual-use items intended for a nuclear weapons programme, and of equipment or software for that purpose
Article 3ter
Transporting a fugitive - unlawfully and intentionally transporting a person on board knowing that they have committed a listed offence and intending to assist them to evade criminal prosecution
Article 3quater
Inchoate and secondary liability for the new offences - attempt, participation as an accomplice, organizing or directing others, and contributing to a group acting with a common purpose
Article 8bis
The boarding regime - dealt with at section 14, because it is enforcement rather than offence-creation

blocks.p: The analytical point the examiner is reaching for is a single sentence: 1988 treats the ship as the target; 2005 treats the ship as the weapon or the delivery vehicle. The 1988 offences all describe harm done to a ship or on board her; the 2005 offences describe harm done by means of a ship to people and places that may be nowhere near the sea. That shift tracks the change in the threat picture between the mid-1980s and the years after 2001, and it is why the proliferation limb - carrying the material rather than using it - appears at all.

blocks.h: 7. How the scheme aims to enhance maritime security

blocks.p: Four mechanisms, and they are worth separating because 'it makes shipping safer' is not an answer.

ul: It closes the impunity gap. Because every Party must criminalize the conduct and must either extradite or prosecute, there is no longer a jurisdiction in which an offender can simply arrive and be beyond reach. That is the Convention's central contribution.
It deters. Certainty of prosecution somewhere is a stronger deterrent than severity of punishment in one place, and the Convention manufactures that certainty.

It makes cooperation routine rather than negotiated. Jurisdiction, custody, inquiry, notification, extradition and evidence-sharing are settled in advance, so States are not improvising a legal relationship in the middle of an incident - which is precisely what went wrong in 1985.

Since 2005, it enables interdiction. The article 8bis procedure allows a suspect ship to be boarded at sea with the flag State's authorization, which moves the regime from punishing an act to preventing one.

blocks.p: The contrast that makes this clear is with the ISPS Code. They are complementary and neither substitutes for the other:

rows: Nature
Criminal law and jurisdiction
Preventive security management
Operates
After the act, and across borders
Before the act, on board and in the port facility
Addressed to
States - their legislatures, prosecutors and courts
Ships and port facilities - operators, masters, security officers
Machinery
Offences, jurisdiction, custody, extradition, prosecution
Security assessments and plans, SSO and CSO, security levels, access control, ship security alert system, declaration of security
Enforced by
National courts, with treaty obligations behind them
Flag State certification and port State control

blocks.p: An answer that describes ship security plans and security levels under the heading of SUA has answered the wrong question. Naming the difference explicitly is what earns the analytical marks in limb (a).

blocks.h: (b) The legal obligations and enforcement mechanisms of States Parties

blocks.p: Limb (b) is not a second pass over the offences. It asks what a Party must do, and the answer is six obligations plus one enforcement procedure, each tied to its article.

blocks.h: 8. Obligation one - criminalize and penalize (article 5)

blocks.p: Each Party shall make the offences punishable by appropriate penalties which take into account the grave nature of those offences. This is the foundation and everything else rests on it: extradition presupposes that the conduct is an offence in both States, and prosecution presupposes an offence in the prosecuting State's own law. A Party that has ratified but never legislated has not implemented the Convention, whatever its formal treaty position.

The obligation is one of result and seriousness, not of form. The Convention does not prescribe a sentence, a maximum or a statutory drafting technique; it requires that the penalty reflect gravity, which is what prevents a Party from nominally complying by treating an armed seizure as a minor regulatory infraction.

blocks.h: 9. Obligation two - establish jurisdiction (article 6)

blocks.p: Article 6 requires each Party to take such measures as may be necessary to establish jurisdiction, and it does so in three layers.

rows: Mandatory
The offence is committed against or on board a ship flying the flag of that State at the time
Shall establish
Mandatory
The offence is committed in the territory of that State, including its territorial sea
Shall establish
Mandatory
The offence is committed by a national of that State
Shall establish
Optional

A stateless person whose habitual residence is in that State commits the offence; a national of that State is seized, threatened, injured or killed during the offence; or the offence is committed in an attempt to compel that State to do or abstain from an act
May establish, on notification to the Secretary-General
Residual and mandatory
The alleged offender is present in its territory and it does not extradite them to any Party that has established jurisdiction
Shall establish - the provision that makes article 10 workable

blocks.p: The residual layer is the one to underline. Without it, a Party could find itself obliged to prosecute under article 10 and lack the jurisdiction in its own law to do so. Article 6 and article 10 are designed to interlock, and explaining that interlock is worth more than reciting either alone. The Convention does not exclude any criminal jurisdiction exercised in accordance with national law.

blocks.h: 10. Obligation three - custody, preliminary inquiry and notification (article 7)

blocks.p: Where an alleged offender is present in a Party's territory, that Party shall, on being satisfied that the circumstances so warrant, take them into custody or take other measures to ensure their presence for such time as is necessary to enable criminal or extradition proceedings to be instituted. It shall immediately make a preliminary inquiry into the facts.
Three protections and duties run alongside:

ul: The person in custody is entitled to communicate without delay with the nearest appropriate representative of the State of which they are a national, or which is otherwise entitled to protect their rights, and to be visited by a representative of that State.

The Party shall immediately notify the States that have established jurisdiction, and the other interested States, of the fact that the person is in custody and of the circumstances warranting detention.
The Party conducting the preliminary inquiry shall promptly report its findings to those States and indicate whether it intends to exercise jurisdiction.

blocks.p: That last requirement is easy to skip and is doing real work: it forces a Party to declare its intention rather than sit on a detained suspect, which is what allows other interested States to decide whether to seek extradition.

blocks.h: 11. Obligation four - extradite or prosecute (article 10)

blocks.p: This is the provision on which the Convention turns. The Party in whose territory the alleged offender is found shall, if it does not extradite them, be obliged without exception whatsoever and whether or not the offence was committed in its territory, to submit the case without delay to its competent authorities for the purpose of prosecution, through proceedings in accordance with its own law. Those authorities take their decision in the same manner as for any other offence of a grave nature under that State's law.

This is the principle known as aut dedere aut judicare - extradite or prosecute. Its practical effect is the abolition of the safe haven, and it is the direct answer to the 1985 problem. Note what it does not do: it does not oblige a State to convict, and it does not remove prosecutorial discretion. It obliges the State to put the case into the system and to treat it with the seriousness it would give any grave offence of its own. Article 10 also requires fair treatment at all stages, including enjoyment of the rights and guarantees provided by the law of the State in whose territory the person is present.

blocks.h: 12. Obligation five - extradition and mutual legal assistance (articles 11, 12 and 8)

ul: Article 11 - extradition. The offences are deemed to be included as extraditable offences in any extradition treaty existing between Parties, and Parties undertake to include them in every treaty concluded between them. A Party that makes extradition conditional on the existence of a treaty may consider this Convention as the legal basis for extradition in respect of these offences. For the purposes of extradition, the offences are treated as if committed not only where they occurred but also in a place within the jurisdiction of the requesting Party.

Article 12 - mutual legal assistance. Parties shall afford one another the greatest measure of assistance in connection with criminal proceedings brought in respect of the offences, including assistance in obtaining evidence at their disposal that is necessary for the proceedings.

Article 8 - the master's power of delivery. The master of a ship of one Party may deliver to the authorities of any other Party a person whom he has reasonable grounds to believe has committed one of the offences, having given notification of his intention and the reasons, and furnished the evidence in his possession. The receiving Party shall accept the delivery except where it has grounds to consider the Convention inapplicable, in which case it gives reasons.

blocks.p: Article 8 is the provision that connects the treaty to the ship. It is the only place in the Convention where a duty falls on a master rather than on a State, and it is the mechanism by which an offender detained on board is transferred into the criminal process. A Chief Engineer's practical interest in this Convention is largely here: the ship secures the person and the evidence, and the master hands both over.

blocks.h: 13. Obligation six - prevention, cooperation and reporting (articles 13 and 14)

ul: Article 13 - Parties shall cooperate in the prevention of the offences, particularly by taking all practicable measures to prevent preparations in their respective territories for the commission of those offences within or outside their territories, and by exchanging information in accordance with their national law and coordinating administrative and other measures to prevent the offences.

Article 14 - any Party having reason to believe that an offence will be committed shall, in accordance with its national law, furnish as promptly as possible any relevant information in its possession to those States which it believes would be the States having established jurisdiction. Parties also report to the Secretary-General of IMO information concerning the offences and the proceedings taken, which the Secretary-General circulates.

blocks.p: The reporting duty is what converts individual national prosecutions into a shared picture. It is the same architectural idea that appears in SOLAS regulation XI-1/6 and the Casualty Investigation Code - the incident is dealt with nationally, and the lesson is shared through IMO - and drawing that parallel is a legitimate way to show breadth in a paper that asks about both.

blocks.h: 14. The enforcement mechanism at sea - boarding under article 8bis

blocks.p: The 2005 Protocol added the only mechanism in the Convention that operates on the water rather than in a courtroom, and it must be stated with its limits or it becomes wrong.

ol: A Party that suspects a listed offence is being, has been or is about to be committed involving a ship flying another Party's flag may request confirmation of nationality from the flag State.

If nationality is confirmed, the requesting Party shall request authorization from the flag State to board the ship, search her and question those on board to determine whether an offence has been or is about to be committed.
The flag State decides. It may authorize the boarding; it may conduct the boarding itself; it may do so jointly with the requesting Party; or it may decline. It may attach conditions.

A Party may notify the Secretary-General that it grants standing authorization - either that boarding is authorized if no reply is received within a stated period, or that boarding and search are authorized generally.

Safeguards apply. The Convention requires due regard for the safety of life at sea and the safety of the ship and cargo, for the commercial and legal interests of the flag State, and for the environment; that the use of force be avoided except when necessary for the safety of those on board and no more than reasonably necessary in the circumstances; that persons on board be treated with due regard for human rights and human dignity; and that a Party is liable for damage, harm or loss attributable to it where the grounds prove unfounded or the measures were unlawful or exceeded what was reasonably required.

blocks.p: The flag State's primacy is preserved throughout, and saying so is what separates a correct answer from an overstated one. Article 8bis creates a structured route to consent; it does not create a right of interdiction. Nothing in it affects the jurisdiction, rights or obligations of States under the general law of the sea.

Read as a whole, then, the Convention gives a Party a complete sequence: it must make the conduct criminal and punish it seriously, take jurisdiction on several bases, secure and inquire into a suspect found on its soil, tell the interested States what it intends, and either send them for trial or try them itself - and, since 2005, it may ask a flag State for permission to stop the ship before any of that becomes necessary. The offences give the Convention its reach; the obligations give it its teeth.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: The two limbs are printed at 8 and 8, and the single most expensive mistake on this question is to answer the offences twice. Limb (a) asks for objectives and key provisions - that is where the offences live, because the offences ARE the Convention's key provisions. Limb (b) asks for legal obligations and enforcement mechanisms that signatory states must implement - that is articles 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14 and 8bis, and if you have spent limb (b) re-describing article 3 you have written half a paper.

Give limb (a) an opening line about the gap piracy leaves. It costs two sentences and it makes everything after it read as purposive rather than descriptive. Then number the article 3 offences - all seven, not a selection, because a partial list reads as partial knowledge on a question where the examiner asked for the key provisions. Then close limb (a) with the ISPS contrast, which is where the word 'how' in the printed stem is pointing.

Limb (b) should be written as six numbered duties plus the boarding procedure. Numbering matters here more than usual: the examiner is looking for coverage across the obligation articles, and a flowing paragraph that mentions extradition and jurisdiction without separating them will be marked as one point, not two.

blocks.h: The idea underneath the Convention

blocks.p: A treaty of this kind is doing something quite specific and rather elegant. It does not create an international court, it does not create an international police force, and it does not give any State a right to act on another's ships. What it does is make national legal systems interoperable for one class of conduct. Every Party writes the same offences into its own criminal law; every Party takes jurisdiction on the same agreed bases; every Party agrees in advance to the same procedure for custody, inquiry and notification; and every Party accepts that if the offender turns up on its territory it will either hand him over or try him.

The result is that the offender can no longer arbitrage the differences between legal systems. Before 1988 the practical question after an incident was 'is there anywhere that both can and must deal with this?' and the answer was often no. After 1988 the answer is always yes, and the only remaining question is which Party. That is a smaller-sounding achievement than it is: the removal of the safe haven is the whole point, and everything in the Convention is either defining the conduct that triggers it or building the machinery that delivers it.

The 2005 extension follows the same logic applied to a changed threat. Once you accept that a ship can be a weapon or a means of moving weapons, the same three questions arise - what conduct, whose jurisdiction, and who is obliged to act - and the Protocol answers them the same way, adding one genuinely new thing: a way to get on board before the harm occurs, with the flag State's consent.

blocks.h: The offence structure, and the phrase that ties it together

blocks.p: Article 3's seven limbs look like a miscellany until you notice that almost all of them end in the same qualification: the conduct must be likely to endanger the safe navigation of the ship. That is the organising principle, and it explains both what is in and what is out.

rows: Armed seizure of the ship
In
Seizure by force is an offence in itself - no endangerment qualification is needed
Assault on a crew member in a bar ashore
Out
Not on board, and not connected with the ship's navigation
Assault on the officer of the watch under way
In
An act of violence on board likely to endanger safe navigation
Stealing a laptop from a cabin
Out
Ordinary theft - engages the flag State's general criminal law, not the Convention
Cutting the ship's steering control cables
In
Damage likely to endanger safe navigation
A hoax distress or navigational broadcast that puts a ship in danger
In
Communicating information known to be false, thereby endangering safe navigation
Damaging a lighthouse or a buoyed channel's markers
In
