blocks.p: If you can apply that test to an unseen scenario you can answer any variant of this question, including the ones that give you a fact pattern rather than asking for a list.

blocks.h: How the obligation articles interlock

blocks.p: Learn these five as a chain rather than as a list, because they were drafted to work in sequence and the sequence is what an examiner recognises as understanding.

ol: Article 5 makes the conduct a crime in national law. Without this, nothing downstream is possible.
Article 6 gives the State the jurisdiction to try it - including, crucially, the residual head that applies precisely when the State would not otherwise have any connection to the offence.
Article 7 secures the person and establishes the facts, and requires the State to say what it intends to do.
Article 11 and 12 make it possible to send the case elsewhere - extraditable offences, the Convention itself as a legal basis, and assistance with evidence.
Article 10 closes the loop: if you do not send him, you must submit the case for prosecution yourself.

blocks.p: Notice that article 10 would be unenforceable without article 6's residual head, and article 6's residual head would be pointless without article 10. That mutual dependence is the most sophisticated observation available on this question and it takes one sentence.

blocks.h: Article 8bis - stating it correctly

blocks.p: This is where good candidates overreach. The temptation is to describe article 8bis as a right to board suspicious ships, and that is simply wrong. The structure is: request confirmation of nationality → request authorization → the flag State decides. The flag State may board itself, board jointly, authorize, impose conditions, or refuse. The only softening is the standing authorization a Party may notify to the Secretary-General - either a general authorization or one that operates if no reply is received within a stated period - and even that is the flag State's own choice, made in advance.

The safeguards are worth a line because they show why the provision was acceptable to flag States at all: safety of life, of the ship and of the cargo; the commercial and legal interests of the flag State; avoidance of force except where necessary and then no more than reasonable; human rights and dignity of those on board; and liability for damage where the grounds prove unfounded. Sovereignty over ships is not a technicality to a flag State, and article 8bis was negotiated in that knowledge.

blocks.h: The evidence position on this question, stated plainly

blocks.p: MIW holds no copy of the SUA Convention or of either 2005 Protocol. That is why this answer names articles and describes their effect but quotes nothing and asserts no sub-paragraph numbering below article level, and why it gives adoption and entry-into-force as years rather than as full dates. It is also why no number of States Parties appears, no percentage of world tonnage, and no Indian implementing statute or section.

If you are revising from this answer, treat the article numbers as reliable at article level and the substance as reliable in effect. If you need to quote the Convention - in a dissertation, or in professional work - obtain the text. In the examination room, naming the article and stating what it does is exactly what earns the mark; quoting it earns nothing extra and inventing a sub-paragraph number can cost you.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: Describing ISPS. Ship security plans, security levels, the SSO, the CSO, the declaration of security and the ship security alert system are SOLAS chapter XI-2 and the ISPS Code. None of them is in the SUA Convention. Mentioning ISPS by way of contrast is excellent; mentioning it by way of answer is fatal.
Saying SUA lets warships stop suspect vessels. It does not. Article 8bis is a consent procedure and the flag State decides.
Writing limb (b) as the offences again. The commonest structural failure on this question.
Inventing article sub-paragraphs. 'Article 3(1)(a)(ii)' looks authoritative and is exactly the kind of detail that is wrong more often than not. Name the article, describe the conduct.
Quoting a number of States Parties. It changes constantly, you cannot check it, and it adds nothing to the answer.

Reaching for the Merchant Shipping Act 2025. It commenced on 15 March 2026, nineteen months after this sitting. For an August 2024 paper the Indian statute is the Merchant Shipping Act 1958 - and in any event the stem does not ask for national law.

blocks.h: If you only have ten minutes for this question

blocks.p: Limb (a), six lines: piracy needs two ships and private ends, so the Achille Lauro fell through the gap and nobody was obliged to act; SUA 1988, in force 1992, extended by the 2005 Protocol in force 2010; its objectives are to criminalize the conduct everywhere, to remove the safe haven, to provide a cooperation framework and to deter; article 3 makes it an offence to seize the ship by force, to commit violence on board likely to endanger safe navigation, to damage or destroy her, to plant a device, to interfere with navigational facilities, to communicate false information endangering navigation, or to injure or kill in connection with any of these, plus attempt, abetting and threat; 2005 added the ship as a weapon and the carriage of weapons of mass destruction, transporting fugitives, and a boarding procedure; and it enhances security by removing impunity and enabling interdiction, as distinct from ISPS, which prevents the incident rather than punishing it.

Limb (b), six lines: make the offences crimes with penalties reflecting their grave nature; establish jurisdiction on the flag, territorial and nationality bases, plus the residual head where the offender is present and is not extradited; take custody, hold a preliminary inquiry, allow consular access, notify the interested States and say whether you will exercise jurisdiction; extradite or prosecute, without exception whatsoever; treat the offences as extraditable, use the Convention itself as a legal basis if you need one, and give the greatest measure of mutual legal assistance; cooperate in prevention and report to the interested States and to the IMO Secretary-General; and note that a master may deliver a suspected offender to another Party's authorities, and that article 8bis permits boarding a foreign ship only with the flag State's authorization, with safeguards.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

blocks.p: These are the places this particular question goes wrong, taken from the ambiguities identified before drafting and from the single error most likely to cost marks.

The one that costs most: Answering as though SUA were a shipboard security regime. It is not - it creates no ship security plan, no ship security officer, no security levels and no declaration of security. Those are ISPS. SUA is a criminal-law and jurisdiction treaty that operates through national courts. The second trap is writing limb (b) as a second pass over the offences: the stem asks what STATES MUST IMPLEMENT, which is articles 5, 6, 7, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14 and the article 8bis boarding procedure.
The wording of the stem invites four specific misreadings, and each is resolved in the answer rather than left to chance:

ul: 'Signatory states' is loose. Strictly, signature and ratification are different acts and the obligations bind States PARTIES rather than signatories. The answer uses 'Party' where precision matters and does not make an issue of the stem's wording, because the examiner plainly means States bound by the Convention.

'Its 2005 Protocol' is printed in the singular. There are in fact TWO 2005 Protocols, one to the Convention and one to the Fixed Platforms Protocol. The answer treats the Convention Protocol as the subject, which is plainly what is meant, and mentions the fixed-platform companion once so that the completeness is visible without derailing the answer.

'Key provisions' in limb (a) overlaps 'legal obligations' in limb (b), and a careless answer will write the same material twice. The division taken is that limb (a) carries the OFFENCE-CREATING provisions - what the Convention makes criminal - and limb (b) carries the OBLIGATION-IMPOSING provisions - what a Party must do about them. Article 8bis sits in limb (b) because it is enforcement, and the stem's second limb names enforcement expressly.

The boarding regime is not an obligation in the same sense as article 10; it is a permission with safeguards. It is placed in limb (b) as the enforcement mechanism, and its consent requirement is stated plainly so that it is not mistaken for a right of interdiction.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

blocks.p: The retrieval questions below are the ones this answer is built to survive. They are the same questions an examiner reaches for when testing whether a written answer was understood or reproduced.

ul: Give the route for the SUA objectives, provisions, obligations and enforcement question. — 8 + 8. The offences belong in limb (a) as 'key provisions'; limb (b) is what a Party must DO. Writing the offences twice is the commonest way to lose half of limb (b).
Why was SUA needed when piracy was already an international crime? — The single best opening for this question. The objectives are unintelligible until the gap is named, and it costs two lines.

What conduct does article 3 of the 1988 Convention make an offence? — Given by identity and effect. MIW holds no text of the Convention, so nothing here is a quotation and no sub-paragraph number is asserted.
What did the 2005 Protocol add? — The shift is from THE SHIP AS TARGET to THE SHIP AS WEAPON OR DELIVERY VEHICLE. Say that sentence and the analytical marks follow.
What must a State Party actually do under the Convention? — This IS limb (b). Six numbered duties, one article each, and the examiner can tick them.
Does the SUA Convention allow one State to board another State's ship? — The commonest overstatement on this question. Saying 'with flag State consent' turns a wrong answer into a right one.

SUA or ISPS - which does what? — The stem asks how SUA enhances maritime security. The honest answer is deterrence and the removal of impunity, and that only becomes clear against the regime it is NOT.

What is aut dedere aut judicare and where is it in the Convention? — If you write one Latin phrase in this paper, write this one - and then explain it in English, because the explanation is what carries the mark.

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: The route, chunked: Limb (a) is GAP (1), DATES (2), OBJECTIVES (3), WHERE (4), OFFENCES 88 (5), OFFENCES 05 (6), SO WHAT (7). Limb (b) is SIX DUTIES plus BOARDING: CRIMINALIZE (8), JURISDICTION (9), CUSTODY (10), TRY-OR-SEND (11), EXTRADITE AND ASSIST (12), PREVENT AND REPORT (13), BOARD WITH CONSENT (14).

Fifteen-second recall: SUA 1988 fills the gap piracy leaves: no second ship, political motive, no duty to prosecute. Adopted Rome 1988, in force 1992; 2005 Protocol in force 2010. Article 3 offences: seize by force, violence endangering navigation, destroy or damage, place a device, interfere with nav aids, false information, injure or kill in connection - plus attempt, abet, threat. 2005 adds 3bis (ship as weapon, WMD transport), 3ter (transporting a fugitive), 3quater, and 8bis boarding with FLAG STATE CONSENT. State duties: 5 penalize, 6 jurisdiction, 7 custody and inquiry, 8 master may deliver, 10 EXTRADITE OR PROSECUTE, 11 extradition, 12 mutual assistance, 13 prevention, 14 report to IMO.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Two limbs at 8 marks each. Limb (a) has two demands joined by 'and how': the PRIMARY OBJECTIVES AND KEY PROVISIONS, and then HOW THEY AIM TO ENHANCE MARITIME SECURITY. The second half is analytical and is where candidates run out of paper. Limb (b) is the operative half and its wording is precise: the LEGAL OBLIGATIONS and the ENFORCEMENT MECHANISMS that SIGNATORY STATES MUST IMPLEMENT. That is a question about what a Party has to do in its own law and at sea, not a second pass over the offence list. A candidate who answers limb (b) by re-listing the offences has answered limb (a) twice.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 8 + 8. In limb (a), roughly one mark for the gap the Convention closes, one for the instruments and dates, two for the objectives, two for the article 3 offences as key provisions, one for the 2005 additions, and one to two for the analytical 'how they enhance maritime security' including the ISPS contrast. In limb (b), roughly one mark each for criminalization and penalties, jurisdiction, custody and inquiry, extradite-or-prosecute, extradition and mutual assistance, prevention and IMO reporting, with two for the article 8bis boarding regime, which is the enforcement mechanism the stem's second noun is pointing at.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That the candidate knows why the Convention was needed at all - that piracy is defined too narrowly to catch a politically motivated attack by people already on board - can identify the principal offences, knows that 2005 added terrorism and proliferation offences and a flag-State-consent boarding procedure, and above all can state what a Party must actually DO: criminalize, penalize, establish jurisdiction, take custody, inquire, notify, and either extradite or prosecute. The aut dedere aut judicare obligation is the single proposition an examiner most wants to see, because it is what makes the Convention work.

decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: LOW - And genuinely so. The 1988 Convention has been in force since 1992 and the 2005 Protocol since 2010. Nothing in the SUA regime moved in 2024, and the donor three months later reaches the same conclusion independently. The real risk on this question is not currency but FABRICATION - with no held text, the temptation is to invent article numbers, party counts and implementing statutes. That risk is controlled by citing only what the answer can carry honestly and by declaring the gap.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: MEDIUM. The Convention operates entirely through national implementation, which invites an Indian statutory limb the stem does not ask for. None is written, because MIW holds no supporting material. The Merchant Shipping Act 1958 governs at this sitting; the Merchant Shipping Act 2025 commenced 15 March 2026 and must not appear.
technical_ambiguities: 'Signatory states' is loose. Strictly, signature and ratification are different acts and the obligations bind States PARTIES rather than signatories. The answer uses 'Party' where precision matters and does not make an issue of the stem's wording, because the examiner plainly means States bound by the Convention.

'Its 2005 Protocol' is printed in the singular. There are in fact TWO 2005 Protocols, one to the Convention and one to the Fixed Platforms Protocol. The answer treats the Convention Protocol as the subject, which is plainly what is meant, and mentions the fixed-platform companion once so that the completeness is visible without derailing the answer.

'Key provisions' in limb (a) overlaps 'legal obligations' in limb (b), and a careless answer will write the same material twice. The division taken is that limb (a) carries the OFFENCE-CREATING provisions - what the Convention makes criminal - and limb (b) carries the OBLIGATION-IMPOSING provisions - what a Party must do about them. Article 8bis sits in limb (b) because it is enforcement, and the stem's second limb names enforcement expressly.

The boarding regime is not an obligation in the same sense as article 10; it is a permission with safeguards. It is placed in limb (b) as the enforcement mechanism, and its consent requirement is stated plainly so that it is not mistaken for a right of interdiction.

questions.understand_first: Think about what the law could and could not reach before this Convention existed. The old crime of piracy was built around a picture of one ship attacking another for private gain, on the high seas. That picture leaves an enormous hole. If the people who seize a ship are already on board - passengers, or crew - there is no second ship. If their motive is political rather than plunder, it is not for private ends. And if they leave the ship in a port and step ashore in a State that has no connection to the incident at all, that State may have no law under which to try them and no obligation to hand them over. A ship could be taken by force, people could be killed, and the offenders could end up somewhere that could not prosecute and did not have to extradite. The answer was to stop trying to stretch piracy and instead write a treaty that does three things in sequence: it defines the conduct - seizing a ship by force, violence on board that endangers her safe navigation, damaging her or planting something that will, interfering with navigational aids, sending false signals; it makes every Party turn that conduct into a crime in its own law with serious penalties and wide jurisdiction; and it removes the escape route by requiring a Party that finds the offender on its soil to either send him for trial elsewhere or try him itself. Later, after attacks that showed the ship could be the weapon rather than the target, the treaty was extended to cover using a ship to cause death or damage, carrying weapons of mass destruction or their materials, and carrying fugitives - and it added a procedure for one State to board another State's ship with that State's consent. It is worth keeping this separate in your head from the shipboard security regime: that one is about keeping the wrong people off the ship in the first place, and this one is about what happens legally once they are on.

quick_revision.major_trap: Answering as though SUA were a shipboard security regime. It is not - it creates no ship security plan, no ship security officer, no security levels and no declaration of security. Those are ISPS. SUA is a criminal-law and jurisdiction treaty that operates through national courts. The second trap is writing limb (b) as a second pass over the offences: the stem asks what STATES MUST IMPLEMENT, which is articles 5, 6, 7, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14 and the article 8bis boarding procedure.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the SUA objectives, provisions, obligations and enforcement question.
retrieval_cards.answer: Limb (a): 1 the gap piracy leaves. 2 the instruments and dates. 3 objectives. 4 where it applies. 5 the 1988 offences. 6 the 2005 additions. 7 how it enhances security, with the ISPS contrast. Limb (b): 8 criminalize and penalize. 9 jurisdiction. 10 custody, inquiry, notification. 11 extradite or prosecute. 12 extradition and mutual assistance. 13 prevention and IMO reporting. 14 boarding under article 8bis.
retrieval_cards.why: 8 + 8. The offences belong in limb (a) as 'key provisions'; limb (b) is what a Party must DO. Writing the offences twice is the commonest way to lose half of limb (b).

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why was SUA needed when piracy was already an international crime?
retrieval_cards.answer: Piracy is built around one ship attacking another for private ends on the high seas. The Achille Lauro seizure in 1985 fitted none of it: the offenders were already on board as passengers, so there was no second ship; their motive was political, so it was not for private ends; and no treaty then obliged the State where they surfaced either to try them or to hand them over. SUA abandons the two-ship and private-ends requirements and replaces them with conduct-based offences plus a duty to extradite or prosecute.
retrieval_cards.why: The single best opening for this question. The objectives are unintelligible until the gap is named, and it costs two lines.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What conduct does article 3 of the 1988 Convention make an offence?
retrieval_cards.answer: Unlawfully and intentionally: seizing or exercising control over a ship by force, threat or intimidation; performing an act of violence against a person on board if it is likely to endanger the safe navigation of the ship; destroying a ship or causing damage to her or her cargo likely to endanger safe navigation; placing or causing to be placed on a ship a device or substance likely to destroy or damage her; destroying, seriously damaging or seriously interfering with maritime navigational facilities where that is likely to endanger safe navigation; communicating information known to be false and thereby endangering safe navigation; and injuring or killing a person in connection with any of these. Attempt, abetting and certain threats are also offences.
retrieval_cards.why: Given by identity and effect. MIW holds no text of the Convention, so nothing here is a quotation and no sub-paragraph number is asserted.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What did the 2005 Protocol add?
retrieval_cards.answer: Three new offence articles and one procedural article. Article 3bis covers using a ship itself as a weapon - to cause death, serious injury or damage for the purpose of intimidating a population or compelling a government - and the transport of explosive or radioactive material, biological, chemical or nuclear weapons and certain dual-use material. Article 3ter covers transporting a person who has committed a listed offence in order to help them evade prosecution. Article 3quater covers attempt, participation and threat in relation to the new offences. Article 8bis creates a boarding procedure.
retrieval_cards.why: The shift is from THE SHIP AS TARGET to THE SHIP AS WEAPON OR DELIVERY VEHICLE. Say that sentence and the analytical marks follow.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What must a State Party actually do under the Convention?
retrieval_cards.answer: Six things. Make the offences crimes under its own law and punish them with penalties reflecting their grave nature (article 5). Establish jurisdiction over them - mandatorily where the ship is flying its flag, where the offence occurs in its territory, and where the offender is its national, with optional further bases (article 6). Take an alleged offender present in its territory into custody or secure their presence, conduct a preliminary inquiry, and notify the interested States (article 7). Either extradite or submit the case to its own prosecuting authorities (article 10). Treat the offences as extraditable and afford mutual legal assistance (articles 11 and 12). Cooperate in prevention and report to the IMO Secretary-General (articles 13 and 14).
retrieval_cards.why: This IS limb (b). Six numbered duties, one article each, and the examiner can tick them.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does the SUA Convention allow one State to board another State's ship?
retrieval_cards.answer: Not unilaterally. Article 8bis permits a Party that suspects a listed offence to request confirmation of nationality and, if confirmed, to request AUTHORIZATION FROM THE FLAG STATE to board, search and question. The flag State may grant it, may board itself, may do so jointly, or may decline. A Party may notify the Secretary-General of standing authorizations, and safeguards govern the use of force, the safety of the ship and cargo, and the treatment of those on board. The flag State's primacy is preserved.
retrieval_cards.why: The commonest overstatement on this question. Saying 'with flag State consent' turns a wrong answer into a right one.

retrieval_cards.prompt: SUA or ISPS - which does what?
retrieval_cards.answer: ISPS, given force by SOLAS chapter XI-2, is PREVENTIVE and operates before and during the voyage: ship and port facility security assessments and plans, a ship security officer and a company security officer, security levels, access control, the ship security alert system and the declaration of security. SUA is CRIMINAL and JURISDICTIONAL and operates after the act and across borders: it defines offences, requires them to be crimes in national law, allocates jurisdiction, and compels prosecution or extradition. Neither substitutes for the other - ISPS aims to stop the incident, SUA ensures it can be punished.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem asks how SUA enhances maritime security. The honest answer is deterrence and the removal of impunity, and that only becomes clear against the regime it is NOT.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is aut dedere aut judicare and where is it in the Convention?
retrieval_cards.answer: Article 10 - the extradite-or-prosecute obligation. A Party in whose territory the alleged offender is found must, if it does not extradite them, submit the case without exception whatsoever and without undue delay to its competent authorities for the purpose of prosecution, whether or not the offence was committed in its territory. It is the provision that removes the safe haven, and it is the mechanism on which the whole Convention turns.
retrieval_cards.why: If you write one Latin phrase in this paper, write this one - and then explain it in English, because the explanation is what carries the mark.

blocks.h: (a) The applicable SOLAS and MARPOL provisions (4 marks)

blocks.p: Answer this limb in three short paragraphs and move on. Four marks will not pay for an essay, and the marks are for naming the right provisions and saying what each does.

blocks.h: 1. SOLAS regulation I/21 - Casualties

blocks.p: The general undertaking. Each Administration undertakes to conduct an investigation of any casualty occurring to any of its ships subject to the provisions of the Convention when it judges that such an investigation may assist in determining what changes in the present regulations might be desirable. Each Contracting Government further undertakes to supply the Organization with pertinent information concerning the findings of such investigations, and the Convention provides that no report or recommendation of the Organization based on that information shall disclose the identity or nationality of the ships concerned or in any manner fix or imply responsibility on any ship or person.

Two features of I/21 are worth a clause each. It is expressed as an undertaking and it is qualified by the Administration's own judgement - when it judges that the investigation may assist. On its own, therefore, it does not compel an investigation into any particular casualty. And the anti-attribution rule in its second paragraph is the earliest expression of the no-blame principle that the Code later develops.

blocks.h: 2. SOLAS regulation XI-1/6 - Additional requirements for the investigation of marine casualties and incidents

blocks.p: This is the provision that turns the undertaking into a method, and it is the one the rest of the question depends on. Taking into account regulation I/21, each Administration shall conduct investigations of marine casualties and incidents in accordance with the Convention as supplemented by the Casualty Investigation Code adopted by resolution MSC.255(84), and:

ol: the provisions of parts I and II of the Code shall be fully complied with;
the related guidance and explanatory material in part III should be taken into account to the greatest possible extent, in order to achieve a more uniform implementation of the Code;

amendments to parts I and II shall be adopted, brought into force and take effect in accordance with article VIII of the Convention - the amendment procedure applicable to the annex other than chapter I; and
part III shall be amended by the Maritime Safety Committee in accordance with its rules of procedure.

blocks.p: Sub-paragraphs .3 and .4 are worth noticing because they are the mechanism by which the Code's two halves have different legal characters: the mandatory half moves by treaty amendment, the recommended half by committee decision. That is the structural reason Part III is guidance.

Note also that regulation I/21 carries a footnote directing the reader to regulation XI-1/6. The two are meant to be read together, and an answer that gives only one of them has given half of limb (a).

blocks.h: 3. MARPOL article 12

blocks.p: MARPOL carries the corresponding duty for pollution casualties at article 12: the obligation on a Party to conduct an investigation of a casualty occurring to any of its ships and to supply the Organization with the relevant findings. The Casualty Investigation Code's own preamble recites SOLAS regulation I/21, MARPOL article 12 and article 23 of the International Convention on Load Lines, 1966 together, as the conventional provisions requiring casualty investigation and the supply of findings - which is why an answer that names all three, rather than only SOLAS, is a complete one.
MIW holds no text-bearing copy of MARPOL, so article 12 is cited here by identity and effect and is not quoted.

blocks.h: (b) The salient points of the Code, and the recommended practices (8 marks)
4. What the Code is, and how it is built

blocks.p: The full title is the Code of the International Standards and Recommended Practices for a Safety Investigation into a Marine Casualty or Marine Incident, known as the Casualty Investigation Code. It was adopted by resolution MSC.255(84) on 16 May 2008 and took effect on 1 January 2010, on the entry into force of the amendments to regulation XI-1/6 that were adopted by the companion resolution MSC.257(84).

It replaced the practice established by the Code for the Investigation of Marine Casualties and Incidents, resolution A.849(20) of 1997, as enhanced by A.884(21) of 1999, which had itself consolidated a chain of Assembly resolutions running back to A.173(ES.IV) in 1968. The essential change in 2008 was of legal character rather than of technique: what had been a recommendation became, in its first two parts, mandatory.

1 to 3

Mandatory (with Part II under XI-1/6)

blocks.h: 5. The purpose - and what a marine safety investigation is not

blocks.p: Chapter 1 states the objective: to provide a common approach for States to adopt in the conduct of marine safety investigations into marine casualties and marine incidents. It then says the thing that defines the whole regime:

ul: Marine safety investigations do not seek to apportion blame or determine liability. A marine safety investigation is conducted with the objective of preventing marine casualties and marine incidents in the future.

The aim is achieved through States applying a consistent methodology and approach, to enable and encourage a broad-ranging investigation in the interests of uncovering causal factors and other safety risks; and providing reports to the Organization so that information is widely disseminated to assist the industry in addressing safety issues.

A marine safety investigation should be separate from, and independent of, any other form of investigation. But the Code does not preclude other investigations - civil, criminal or administrative - and, importantly, it is not the intent of the Code that a State should refrain from fully reporting on the causal factors because blame or liability may be inferred from the findings.

blocks.p: That last clause is the sophisticated part and it is worth a sentence in the exam. The Code does not promise that nobody will be blamed as a result of what an investigation finds; it promises that blame is not the investigation's purpose, and it forbids an investigating State from softening its findings out of concern for the consequences.

Chapter 1 also records the jurisdictional starting point: each flag State has a duty to investigate any casualty to a ship flying its flag where it judges the investigation may assist in determining desirable regulatory changes or where the casualty has produced a major deleterious effect on the environment; a flag State shall cause an inquiry into certain casualties and incidents of navigation on the high seas; and a State in whose territory, including territorial sea, a casualty occurs has a right to investigate where it might pose a risk to life or the environment, involve its search and rescue authorities, or otherwise affect it as coastal State.

blocks.h: 6. Mandatory standards - the Authority, and notification

blocks.p: Chapter 4 is a single obligation: the Government of each State shall provide the Organization with detailed contact information of the marine safety investigation Authority or Authorities carrying out investigations within their State. Simple, and the precondition for everything else - other States must know whom to contact.
Chapter 5 - notification.

rows: On the high seas or in an exclusive economic zone
The flag State of the ship or ships involved notifies other substantially interested States, as soon as is reasonably practicable
Within the territory, including the territorial sea, of a coastal State
The flag State and the coastal State notify each other, and between them notify the other substantially interested States, as soon as is reasonably practicable

blocks.p: Notification shall not be delayed due to the lack of complete information, and it contains as much of the following as is readily available: the name of the ship and its flag State; the IMO ship identification number; the nature of the casualty; its location; the time and date; the number of any seriously injured or killed persons; the consequences to individuals, property and the environment; and the identification of any other ship involved.

blocks.h: 7. Mandatory standards - the duty to investigate, and agreement between States

blocks.p: Chapter 6 is the operative obligation of the whole Code and it is short enough to know exactly:

ul: A marine safety investigation shall be conducted into every very serious marine casualty.

Subject to any agreement under chapter 7, the flag State of a ship involved in a very serious marine casualty is responsible for ensuring that a marine safety investigation is conducted and completed in accordance with the Code.

blocks.p: Chapter 7 deals with the practical problem that several States may be entitled or obliged to investigate the same event. Where a casualty occurs in a State's territory, the flag State or States and the coastal State shall consult to seek agreement on which State or States will be the marine safety investigating State. The same duty to consult applies where a casualty on the high seas or in an EEZ involves more than one flag State. Agreement may also be reached with another substantially interested State for that State to investigate. Until agreement is reached - or if it is not reached - the existing obligations and rights of each State remain, and each may conduct its own investigation.

Chapter 7.5 supplies the reason a flag State is willing to hand the work over: by fully participating in a marine safety investigation conducted by another substantially interested State, the flag State shall be considered to fulfil its obligations under the Code, SOLAS regulation I/21 and article 94(7) of UNCLOS. That is the provision which prevents duplicated investigation from being the only safe course.

blocks.h: 8. Mandatory standards - powers, parallel investigations, cooperation, independence

ul: Chapter 8 - powers. All States shall ensure that their national laws provide investigators with the ability to board a ship, interview the master and crew and any other person involved, and acquire evidential material. Without this the Code would be unenforceable in practice, because an investigator with no statutory power of access cannot investigate.

Chapter 9 - parallel investigations. Nothing prejudices the right of another substantially interested State to conduct its own separate investigation; but the States concerned shall seek to co-ordinate the timing of their investigations, to avoid conflicting demands upon witnesses and access to evidence where possible.

Chapter 10 - co-operation. All substantially interested States shall co-operate with the investigating State to the extent practicable, and the investigating State shall provide for their participation to the extent practicable.

Chapter 11 - investigation not to be subject to external direction. Investigating States shall ensure that investigators are impartial and objective, and that the investigation is able to report its results without direction or interference from any persons or organizations that may be affected by its outcome.

blocks.p: Chapter 11 is the structural guarantee of the whole regime. An investigation that can be leaned on by the flag State's own ministry, by the owner, by the class society or by the insurer produces findings nobody can rely on, and the Code therefore makes freedom from direction a mandatory standard rather than an aspiration.

blocks.h: 9. Mandatory standards - obtaining evidence from seafarers

blocks.p: Chapter 12 is the human-element limb and it is the one a serving engineer is most likely to encounter personally.

ul: Evidence shall be taken at the earliest practical opportunity, and the seafarer shall be allowed to return to his or her ship, or be repatriated, at the earliest possible opportunity. The seafarer's human rights shall at all times be upheld.
All seafarers from whom evidence is sought shall be informed of the nature and basis of the investigation.

Further, a seafarer from whom evidence is sought shall be informed of, and allowed access to legal advice regarding: any potential risk of self-incrimination in proceedings subsequent to the investigation; any right not to self-incriminate or to remain silent; and any protections afforded to prevent the evidence being used against them.

blocks.p: This chapter sits alongside the Guidelines on Fair Treatment of Seafarers in the Event of a Maritime Accident, resolution A.987(24), adopted in December 2005 and promulgated jointly by IMO and ILO on 1 July 2006. Together they are the answer to an obvious objection: if a marine safety investigation is genuinely no-blame but the same facts may later be used in a criminal prosecution, a seafarer needs to know precisely where they stand before they speak.

blocks.h: 10. Mandatory standards - draft and final reports

blocks.p: Chapter 13 - draft reports. Where requested, the investigating State shall send a copy of the draft report to a substantially interested State so that it may comment. Two conditions protect the draft: the receiving State must guarantee not to circulate, publish or give access to it without express consent; and the investigating State is not bound to send the draft if it asks the receiving State to affirm that the evidence in it will not be admitted in civil or criminal proceedings against the person who gave it and that affirmation is refused.

Substantially interested States are invited to comment within 30 days or another mutually agreed period. The investigating State shall consider the comments before preparing the final report, and where acceptance or rejection of a comment will directly affect the interests of the State that made it, shall notify that State how the comment was addressed. If no comments arrive within the period, it may proceed to finalise. It shall also seek to fully verify the accuracy and completeness of the draft by the most practical means.
Chapter 14 - final reports.

ul: The final version shall be submitted to the Organization for every marine safety investigation conducted into a very serious marine casualty.

Where an investigation into a casualty or incident other than a very serious marine casualty produces a report containing information which may prevent or lessen the seriousness of future casualties or incidents, the final version shall also be submitted.
The report shall utilise all the information obtained, taking account of the investigation's scope, so that all relevant safety issues are included and understood and safety action can be taken.

The final report shall be made available to the public and the shipping industry by the investigating State, or that State shall undertake to assist the public and the industry with the details necessary to access it where it is published by another State or by the Organization.

blocks.p: What a report must contain is fixed by the definition in Part I: a summary of the basic facts stating whether deaths, injuries or pollution occurred; the identity of the flag State, owners, operators, the company as identified in the safety management certificate and the classification society, subject to national privacy laws; the ship's dimensions and engines and a description of the crew, work routine and time served; a narrative of the circumstances; analysis and comment on the causal factors including mechanical, human and organizational factors; a discussion of the findings, the safety issues identified and the conclusions; and where appropriate, recommendations with a view to preventing future casualties.

blocks.h: 11. Part III - the recommended practices

blocks.p: The stem asks for these expressly, and they are where the marks are that most candidates leave on the table. Part III runs from chapter 15 to chapter 26 and covers:

States should ensure investigating Authorities have sufficient material and financial resources and suitably qualified personnel. Investigators should be appointed on the basis of the skills outlined in resolution A.996(25), without precluding specialists appointed temporarily or consultants for expert advice

The principles on which an investigation should be conducted - independence, systematic method, and the pursuit of causal factors rather than of fault

Investigation of marine casualties other than very serious, and of marine incidents - the discretionary tier

What States should weigh when deciding which of them should investigate

Handling an investigation where the event may be a deliberate act rather than an accident

Notification to the parties involved and the commencement of the investigation

How a multi-State investigation should be run in practice
22 Collection of evidence
Practical guidance on securing and gathering evidential material
23 Confidentiality of information
Protection of the marine safety record - statements, communications, medical and private information, analyses, and voyage data recorder information

Safeguards for those who give evidence

blocks.p: Two of these deserve a line each in an eight-mark limb. Chapter 17 matters because it is the tier where most real investigations sit - below the mandatory VSMC threshold, where investigation is a matter of judgement, and where the Code nevertheless recommends the same method. And chapter 23 matters because the confidentiality of the marine safety record is what makes candid evidence possible at all; without it, chapter 12's protections would be hollow.

blocks.h: (c) The term “very serious marine casualty” (4 marks)
12. The definition

blocks.p: The Code defines it in a single sentence, and it should be given exactly:

ul: A very serious marine casualty means a marine casualty involving the total loss of the ship or a death or severe damage to the environment.

blocks.p: Three points follow immediately from the wording. It is a subset of marine casualty, so the event must first qualify as a marine casualty at all. The three branches are alternatives, not cumulative - any one of them is sufficient. And 'a death' means one; there is no threshold of multiple fatalities.

blocks.h: 13. Reading the definition against its neighbours

blocks.p: Four marks are not paid for one sentence, and the way to earn them is to locate the term in the Code's definition set.

rows: Marine casualty

An event, or sequence of events, that has resulted in any of the following directly in connection with the operations of a ship: the death of, or serious injury to, a person; the loss of a person from a ship; the loss, presumed loss or abandonment of a ship; material damage to a ship; the stranding or disabling of a ship, or her involvement in a collision; material damage to marine infrastructure external to a ship that could seriously endanger the safety of the ship, another ship or an individual; or severe damage to the environment, or the potential for it, brought about by the damage of a ship or ships. It does not include a deliberate act or omission intended to cause harm
Marine incident

An event, or sequence of events, other than a marine casualty, occurring directly in connection with the operations of a ship, which endangered, or if not corrected would endanger, the safety of the ship, its occupants, any other person or the environment. The same exclusion of deliberate acts applies
Very serious marine casualty
A marine casualty involving the total loss of the ship, or a death, or severe damage to the environment
Severe damage to the environment
Damage which, as evaluated by the State or States affected, or the flag State as appropriate, produces a major deleterious effect upon the environment
Serious injury
An injury resulting in incapacitation where the person is unable to function normally for more than 72 hours, commencing within seven days from the date the injury was suffered
Material damage

Damage that significantly affects the structural integrity, performance or operational characteristics of marine infrastructure or a ship and requires major repair or replacement of a major component; or destruction of the infrastructure or ship

blocks.p: Two observations that are worth making because they show the definition has been read rather than remembered. First, serious injury does not make a casualty very serious - a serious injury makes the event a marine casualty; it takes a death to reach the top category. Second, the environmental branch is evaluative rather than objective: it depends on what the affected State or the flag State assesses as a major deleterious effect, so two States could in principle classify the same spill differently.

blocks.h: 14. Why the classification matters

blocks.p: The term is not a label. It is the switch that turns discretion into obligation, and this is where the remaining marks are.

headers: Other marine casualty or marine incident
rows: Investigation
Mandatory - chapter 6: an investigation shall be conducted into every VSMC, and the flag State is responsible for ensuring it is conducted and completed
Discretionary - SOLAS I/21 applies where the Administration judges the investigation may assist; Part III chapter 17 recommends the method where one is held
Report to IMO
Mandatory - chapter 14.1: the final version shall be submitted to the Organization for every VSMC
Conditional - chapter 14.2: submitted where the report contains information that may prevent or lessen the seriousness of future casualties
Notification
Applies to marine casualties generally under chapter 5
Applies to marine casualties generally under chapter 5

blocks.p: So the practical significance is this: the moment an event is classified as a very serious marine casualty, the flag State loses its discretion. It must investigate, it must complete the investigation to the Code's standard, and it must send the report to IMO where it becomes part of the international body of lessons. Below that threshold the same machinery is available and recommended, but whether it is used is a judgement. That is why the definition is examined, and it is why the classification is made carefully at the outset of an incident rather than at the end.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: The printed marks are 4 / 8 / 4 and they are the plan. The most common way to mismanage this question is to write limb (a) at length - it is enjoyable, you know the regulations, and it feels like progress - and then arrive at an eight-mark limb (b) with no time. Limb (a) is a naming task. Three short paragraphs: I/21, XI-1/6, MARPOL article 12. Say what each does in one sentence and stop.

Limb (b) is the paper. Eight marks, and the stem contains a signpost most candidates walk past: it asks for the salient points of the Code and the recommended practices. 'Recommended practices' is the title of Part III. If your limb (b) covers only the mandatory standards you have answered half of it, however well. Give Part II in the Code's own chapter order - it is a sensible order and it stops you forgetting a chapter - and then give Part III as a short block, naming three or four of its chapters.

Limb (c) is four marks for a one-line definition, which tells you the definition alone is not the answer. Give it exactly, then place it against marine casualty, marine incident and severe damage to the environment, then say what the classification triggers. That third step - mandatory investigation under chapter 6 and mandatory report to IMO under chapter 14.1 - is where the last two marks are.

blocks.h: The idea underneath the Code

blocks.p: The regime exists because of a conflict that cannot be resolved, only separated. After a casualty, society wants two incompatible things. It wants accountability, which requires adversarial process, rights against self-incrimination, and a standard of proof. And it wants to learn, which requires people to say frankly what they did wrong, including the things that would embarrass or incriminate them.

You cannot get both from one inquiry. If the inquiry can punish, nobody will be candid. If the inquiry cannot punish, some people will feel justice was not done. The international answer is to run the second kind of inquiry properly and to insulate it: a marine safety investigation whose sole statutory purpose is prevention, which does not apportion blame or determine liability, which is separate from and independent of criminal, civil and administrative proceedings, which cannot be directed by anyone affected by its outcome, and which gives the seafarer explicit notice of the risk of self-incrimination and access to legal advice before they speak.

Everything in the Code follows from that design decision. Chapter 11's freedom from external direction protects the finding. Chapter 12's warnings protect the witness. Chapter 23's confidentiality of the marine safety record protects the candour. Chapter 13's condition - that a State receiving a draft may be asked to affirm the evidence will not be used in proceedings against the person who gave it - protects the whole arrangement internationally. And chapter 14's duty to publish and to submit to IMO is what makes the exercise worth doing at all: an investigation whose lessons stay inside one administration has protected the witness and taught nobody.

blocks.h: Why there are two SOLAS regulations, and what changed in 2010

blocks.p: This is worth understanding rather than memorising, because it explains the shape of limb (a).

Regulation I/21 is old. A provision requiring flag States to investigate casualties where the investigation might assist in identifying regulatory shortcomings appeared in the 1948 SOLAS Convention and was retained in 1960 and 1974, and the Load Lines Convention 1966 carried the same idea. But it is an undertaking, qualified by the Administration's own judgement, and it says nothing about how to investigate, whom to tell, who takes the lead when three countries are involved, or what the report must contain. For decades the 'how' lived in Assembly resolutions - A.173(ES.IV), A.322(IX), A.440(XI), A.442(XI), A.637(16), consolidated into A.849(20) in 1997 and enhanced by A.884(21) in 1999 - all of which were recommendations.

Regulation XI-1/6 is the change. Adopted by MSC.257(84) alongside the Code itself, it takes the old undertaking as its starting point - 'taking into account regulation I/21' - and makes the method binding: Parts I and II of the Code shall be fully complied with. That is what happened on 1 January 2010, and it is why an answer that names only I/21 is describing the pre-2010 world.

blocks.h: The chapter map of Part II, in one pass

blocks.p: If you can reconstruct these eleven chapters you can write limb (b) without notes. They fall into four natural groups.

ul: Who and when - chapter 4 (tell IMO who your investigation Authority is) and chapter 5 (notification: who tells whom, not delayed for incomplete information, eight content items).

Whether and by whom - chapter 6 (a VSMC shall be investigated; the flag State is responsible) and chapter 7 (States consult and agree who investigates; full participation discharges the flag State's obligations under the Code, SOLAS I/21 and UNCLOS article 94(7)).

How it is protected - chapter 8 (national law must give investigators power to board, interview and take evidence), chapter 9 (parallel investigations allowed, timing coordinated), chapter 10 (cooperation and participation), chapter 11 (impartial, objective, free from direction) and chapter 12 (seafarers' evidence and rights).

What comes out - chapter 13 (draft report, confidentiality guarantee, 30 days for comments, verify accuracy) and chapter 14 (final report to IMO for every VSMC, conditionally for lesser events, made available to the public).

blocks.h: The definitions, and the mistakes people make with them

rows: 'A very serious marine casualty involves loss of life and loss of the ship'
Or, not and. Any one of total loss of the ship, a death, or severe damage to the environment
'Several deaths are needed'
A death. One is sufficient
'A serious injury makes it very serious'
No. A serious injury makes the event a marine casualty. Serious injury is defined as incapacitation preventing normal function for more than 72 hours, beginning within seven days of the injury
'Any pollution makes it very serious'
Only severe damage to the environment, which is damage producing a major deleterious effect as evaluated by the affected State or the flag State
'A deliberate act - sabotage, an attack - is a marine casualty'

Expressly excluded. Neither a marine casualty nor a marine incident includes a deliberate act or omission intended to cause harm to the safety of a ship, an individual or the environment. Part III chapter 19 deals separately with acts of unlawful interference
'A near miss is a marine casualty'
It is a marine incident - an event other than a casualty which endangered, or if not corrected would endanger, safety

blocks.p: The deliberate-act exclusion is the single detail that most reliably distinguishes a candidate who has read the definitions. It also connects this question to Q2 on the same paper: conduct intended to cause harm is not a marine casualty at all - it is the subject matter of the SUA Convention.

blocks.h: Practical significance for a Chief Engineer

blocks.p: You are unlikely to conduct a marine safety investigation. You are quite likely to be inside one, and three things in the Code are worth carrying to sea.

ul: Preserve the evidence. The definition of a marine safety record includes statements, communications relating to the operation of the ship, records of analysis, and voyage data recorder information. Bell logbooks, alarm printouts, engine data, oil record books and standing orders are the engineering equivalent, and they are worth more the earlier they are secured.

Know what you are being asked, and by whom. A marine safety investigation is no-blame; a class surveyor, a P&I correspondent, a flag State enforcement officer and a coastal State prosecutor are not conducting one. Chapter 12 entitles you to be told the nature and basis of the investigation, and to be informed of and given access to legal advice about self-incrimination and the right to remain silent.

Expect the report to be public. Chapter 14.4 requires the final report to be made available to the public and the shipping industry. The corollary is that published investigation reports are among the best technical training material available, and reading them is how the system's benefit actually reaches the fleet.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: Naming one SOLAS regulation. There are two, and they do different jobs.
Calling MARPOL article 12 a regulation. MARPOL's articles and its Annexes' regulations are different things; article 12 is an article.
Omitting Part III. The stem asks for the recommended practices by name.

Saying the Code prevents criminal proceedings. It does not. It keeps the safety investigation separate from them, and it protects the safety record and the witness - but the Code expressly does not preclude civil, criminal or administrative investigation.
Saying investigators must avoid findings that imply blame. The opposite: the Code says a State should not refrain from fully reporting causal factors because blame or liability may be inferred.

Importing the Merchant Shipping Act. The stem asks for SOLAS and MARPOL. The Indian machinery is a different question, and the Merchant Shipping Act 2025 did not commence until 15 March 2026 - nineteen months after this sitting.
Giving A.849(20) as the current Code. It was superseded when MSC.255(84) took effect on 1 January 2010. Mention it as history if you like; do not give it as the answer.

blocks.h: If you only have ten minutes for this question

blocks.p: Limb (a), three lines. SOLAS I/21: each Administration undertakes to investigate any casualty to its ships where it judges the investigation may assist in determining desirable regulatory changes, and to supply IMO with the findings. SOLAS XI-1/6: taking I/21 into account, investigations shall be conducted in accordance with the Casualty Investigation Code, MSC.255(84), with Parts I and II fully complied with and Part III taken into account to the greatest possible extent. MARPOL article 12 carries the corresponding duty for pollution casualties, as does Load Lines article 23.

Limb (b), eight lines. The Code was adopted by MSC.255(84) on 16 May 2008 and took effect 1 January 2010, replacing A.849(20); Part I general, Part II mandatory, Part III recommended. Its purpose is prevention and it does not apportion blame or determine liability. Salient mandatory points: tell IMO who your investigation Authority is; notify the substantially interested States promptly and without waiting for complete information; every very serious marine casualty shall be investigated, with the flag State responsible; States consult and agree which will investigate, and full participation discharges the flag State's obligations; national law must give investigators powers to board, interview and take evidence; parallel investigations are permitted but coordinated; investigators must be impartial, objective and free from external direction; seafarers' evidence is taken early with their human rights upheld and with notice of self-incrimination risk and access to legal advice; draft reports go to substantially interested States with 30 days to comment; and the final report goes to IMO for every VSMC and is made public. Recommended practices in Part III: adequate resources and investigators qualified on the A.996(25) skills, principles of investigation, investigation of lesser casualties, acts of unlawful interference, coordination, collection of evidence, confidentiality of the marine safety record, protection of witnesses, and re-opening an investigation.

Limb (c), four lines. A very serious marine casualty is a marine casualty involving the total loss of the ship, or a death, or severe damage to the environment - three alternatives, any one sufficient. It sits inside 'marine casualty', which has seven limbs and excludes deliberate acts, and above 'marine incident', which is an event that endangered or would endanger safety. Severe damage to the environment means a major deleterious effect as evaluated by the affected State or the flag State. The classification matters because it is the trigger: a VSMC must be investigated under chapter 6 and its report must be submitted to IMO under chapter 14.1, whereas below that threshold both are matters of judgement.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

blocks.p: These are the places this particular question goes wrong, taken from the ambiguities identified before drafting and from the single error most likely to cost marks.

The one that costs most: Giving only ONE SOLAS regulation in limb (a). There are two and they do different jobs. The second trap is omitting Part III from limb (b) when the stem expressly asks for 'the recommended practices' - that is Part III's own title and it is a signposted demand. The third is answering limb (c) with a general impression of seriousness instead of the Code's three branches: total loss of the ship, OR a death, OR severe damage to the environment.
The wording of the stem invites four specific misreadings, and each is resolved in the answer rather than left to chance:

ul: 'The applicable regulation of SOLAS' is printed in the singular and there are TWO. Regulation I/21 creates the general undertaking; regulation XI-1/6 is what makes the Casualty Investigation Code mandatory and is the one the rest of the question depends on. The answer gives both and explains the relationship, because giving only I/21 leaves limb (b) unanchored and giving only XI-1/6 misses the provision it expressly takes into account.
MARPOL's provision is an ARTICLE, not a regulation. The stem's word 'regulation' is loose. The answer says article 12 and does not make an issue of the wording.

'Salient points of casualty investigation code AND the recommended practices' could be read as one demand or two. It is two: the Code's mandatory standards are in Part II, and 'recommended practices' is Part III's own title. An answer that stops at Part II has answered the first half of an eight-mark limb.

'Very serious marine casualty' is defined in the Code in a single short sentence, which cannot by itself be worth four marks. The limb is therefore answered by giving the definition exactly, then locating it against marine casualty, marine incident and severe damage to the environment, then explaining what the classification triggers.

The Code's definition of severe damage to the environment is itself evaluative - 'as evaluated by the State(s) affected, or the flag State' - so a VSMC finding on that branch is not purely objective. The answer says so, because it is the honest reading of the text.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

blocks.p: The retrieval questions below are the ones this answer is built to survive. They are the same questions an examiner reaches for when testing whether a written answer was understood or reproduced.

ul: Give the route for the casualty investigation question. — Printed 4/8/4. Limb (a) is a naming task and must stay short; limb (b) is eight marks and needs the Code's own chapter order; limb (c) needs three sections because one line of definition cannot be worth four marks.

Which SOLAS regulations require a flag State to investigate a casualty, and what does each do? — Four marks for limb (a) and half of them are here. I/21 alone is the pre-2010 answer; XI-1/6 alone leaves the Code unanchored.
Define a very serious marine casualty. — The whole of limb (c) rests on getting these three branches right and on knowing they are alternatives, not cumulative.

Marine casualty, marine incident, very serious marine casualty - how do they differ? — The three sit inside each other and limb (c) cannot be answered for four marks without showing where the boundaries are. The deliberate-act exclusion is the detail most candidates miss.
What is a marine safety investigation NOT for? — The single most distinctive feature of the regime and the easiest mark in limb (b). The last clause is the one that shows real understanding.
Who must be told about a marine casualty, and by whom? — A compact, countable list that lifts limb (b) above generalities.

When is an investigation compulsory, and when must the report go to IMO? — This is the payoff of limb (c) and it is what makes the classification worth four marks - VSMC is the trigger for both mandatory duties.

What protections does the Code give a seafarer whose evidence is taken? — The human-element limb of the Code, and the part a Chief Engineer is most likely to meet in person. It is also the answer to 'why would anyone tell an investigator the truth?'

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: The route, chunked: Limb (a) is TWO SOLAS PLUS ONE MARPOL: I/21 general (1), XI-1/6 the Code (2), MARPOL art 12 (3). Limb (b) is WHAT (4), WHY-NOT-BLAME (5), then the Code's own order - TELL (6), MUST INVESTIGATE (7), POWERS AND INDEPENDENCE (8), SEAFARERS (9), REPORTS (10), PART III (11). Limb (c) is DEFINE (12), COMPARE (13), CONSEQUENCE (14).

Fifteen-second recall: Limb (a): SOLAS I/21 (Administration undertakes to investigate any casualty where it may assist in determining desirable regulation changes, and to supply IMO with findings) + SOLAS XI-1/6 (investigations SHALL be in accordance with the Casualty Investigation Code, MSC.255(84); Parts I and II fully complied with, Part III taken into account) + MARPOL article 12. Limb (b): MSC.255(84), adopted 16 May 2008, effective 1 January 2010. Part I general, Part II MANDATORY, Part III recommended. Purpose is prevention, NOT blame or liability. Notify, investigate every VSMC, agree the investigating State, powers to board and interview, no external direction, seafarers' rights, draft report 30 days for comments, final report to IMO for every VSMC and made public. Limb (c): a VSMC is a marine casualty involving TOTAL LOSS OF THE SHIP or A DEATH or SEVERE DAMAGE TO THE ENVIRONMENT.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Three printed limbs with a printed 4/8/4 split, and each is a different kind of task. Limb (a), 4 marks, is a STATE question - name the applicable regulation of SOLAS and of MARPOL. It is short, it is precise, and it must not be allowed to grow. Limb (b), 8 marks and the body of the question, asks for the SALIENT POINTS of the Code AND the RECOMMENDED PRACTICES - two demands, and the second is a deliberate pointer at Part III, which most candidates omit entirely. Limb (c), 4 marks, is a DEFINITION question about a term the Code defines in one line; four marks cannot be earned by reciting that line alone, so the definition must be placed against its neighbours and its consequences explained.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 4 + 8 + 4, printed per limb. In limb (a), roughly two marks for the SOLAS pair - I/21 for the general duty and XI-1/6 for the mandatory Code - and two for MARPOL article 12. In limb (b), roughly one mark for what the Code is and how it is structured, one for its purpose and the no-blame principle, and about five spread across the mandatory standards - notification, the duty to investigate a VSMC, agreement between States, powers, independence, evidence from seafarers, reports - with at least one clearly attributable to Part III, which the stem names as 'recommended practices'. In limb (c), one mark for the definition, one for the surrounding definitions that give it meaning, and two for the consequence - that the classification is what triggers the mandatory duty to investigate and the mandatory report to IMO.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That the candidate can name TWO SOLAS regulations, not one - I/21 is the historic general undertaking and XI-1/6 is what makes the Code mandatory, and an answer that gives only one has half the limb. That the candidate knows the Code by its resolution number and knows which of its parts are mandatory. That the candidate can state the no-blame principle, because it is the single most distinctive feature of a marine safety investigation. That the candidate remembers Part III at all. And that in limb (c) the candidate gives the Code's actual three-branch definition rather than a general impression of seriousness.

technical_ambiguities: 'The applicable regulation of SOLAS' is printed in the singular and there are TWO. Regulation I/21 creates the general undertaking; regulation XI-1/6 is what makes the Casualty Investigation Code mandatory and is the one the rest of the question depends on. The answer gives both and explains the relationship, because giving only I/21 leaves limb (b) unanchored and giving only XI-1/6 misses the provision it expressly takes into account.
MARPOL's provision is an ARTICLE, not a regulation. The stem's word 'regulation' is loose. The answer says article 12 and does not make an issue of the wording.

'Salient points of casualty investigation code AND the recommended practices' could be read as one demand or two. It is two: the Code's mandatory standards are in Part II, and 'recommended practices' is Part III's own title. An answer that stops at Part II has answered the first half of an eight-mark limb.

'Very serious marine casualty' is defined in the Code in a single short sentence, which cannot by itself be worth four marks. The limb is therefore answered by giving the definition exactly, then locating it against marine casualty, marine incident and severe damage to the environment, then explaining what the classification triggers.

The Code's definition of severe damage to the environment is itself evaluative - 'as evaluated by the State(s) affected, or the flag State' - so a VSMC finding on that branch is not purely objective. The answer says so, because it is the honest reading of the text.
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Fourteen numbered sections under three limb headings, proportioned to the printed 4/8/4. Limb (a) takes three short sections and must stay short - it is a naming task. Limb (b) takes eight sections, running from what the Code is, through purpose, through the mandatory standards in the Code's own chapter order, to Part III. Limb (c) takes three sections: the definition itself, the definitions around it in a table, and the consequence. Tables carry the definition set and the notification rules, because both are compact and comparative.

questions.understand_first: When something goes badly wrong on a ship, two completely different questions arise and they pull in opposite directions. One is who is to blame - which is a matter for courts, insurers, prosecutors and disciplinary bodies, and it is settled by evidence tested adversarially. The other is why did this happen and how do we stop it happening again - which needs the opposite conditions entirely, because the people who know most about what went wrong are usually the people most exposed if blame is being allocated, and they will not talk freely if their words will be used against them. If you run only the first kind of inquiry, you get someone punished and you learn nothing transferable. So the international system deliberately separates them. It creates an inquiry whose only purpose is prevention, which expressly does not apportion blame or determine liability, which is independent of any other proceedings, and which is protected from outside direction - and it obliges States to run one whenever the worst class of accident occurs, and to send the report to the Organization so that everyone else can learn from it too. The obligation itself is old and sits in the conventions - the flag State undertakes to investigate and to share what it finds. What is newer is the standard method: a code that says who must be told, who investigates when several countries are involved, what powers investigators need, how seafarers must be treated when their evidence is taken, and what the report has to contain. The threshold that switches the whole thing from discretionary to compulsory is the worst category - the ship lost, a life lost, or the environment badly damaged - and that is the category the third limb is asking you to define.
questions.memory_cue: Limb (a) is TWO SOLAS PLUS ONE MARPOL: I/21 general (1), XI-1/6 the Code (2), MARPOL art 12 (3). Limb (b) is WHAT (4), WHY-NOT-BLAME (5), then the Code's own order - TELL (6), MUST INVESTIGATE (7), POWERS AND INDEPENDENCE (8), SEAFARERS (9), REPORTS (10), PART III (11). Limb (c) is DEFINE (12), COMPARE (13), CONSEQUENCE (14).

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the casualty investigation question.
retrieval_cards.answer: Limb (a): 1 SOLAS I/21. 2 SOLAS XI-1/6. 3 MARPOL article 12. Limb (b): 4 what the Code is and its three parts. 5 purpose and the no-blame principle. 6 notification. 7 the duty to investigate a VSMC and agreement between States. 8 powers, parallel investigations, cooperation, independence. 9 evidence from seafarers. 10 draft and final reports. 11 Part III recommended practices. Limb (c): 12 the definition. 13 the neighbouring definitions. 14 what the classification triggers.
retrieval_cards.why: Printed 4/8/4. Limb (a) is a naming task and must stay short; limb (b) is eight marks and needs the Code's own chapter order; limb (c) needs three sections because one line of definition cannot be worth four marks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which SOLAS regulations require a flag State to investigate a casualty, and what does each do?
retrieval_cards.answer: TWO. Regulation I/21 (Casualties) is the general undertaking: each Administration undertakes to conduct an investigation of any casualty occurring to any of its ships subject to the Convention when it judges that the investigation may assist in determining what changes in the regulations might be desirable, and each Contracting Government undertakes to supply the Organization with pertinent information on the findings. Regulation XI-1/6 (Additional requirements for the investigation of marine casualties and incidents) is what makes the method mandatory: taking into account regulation I/21, each Administration shall conduct investigations in accordance with the Convention as supplemented by the Casualty Investigation Code adopted by MSC.255(84), with Parts I and II to be fully complied with and Part III to be taken into account to the greatest possible extent.
retrieval_cards.why: Four marks for limb (a) and half of them are here. I/21 alone is the pre-2010 answer; XI-1/6 alone leaves the Code unanchored.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define a very serious marine casualty.
retrieval_cards.answer: A very serious marine casualty means a marine casualty involving the TOTAL LOSS OF THE SHIP or A DEATH or SEVERE DAMAGE TO THE ENVIRONMENT. Three alternative branches - any one is sufficient. 'Severe damage to the environment' is itself defined as damage which, as evaluated by the State or States affected or the flag State as appropriate, produces a major deleterious effect upon the environment.
retrieval_cards.why: The whole of limb (c) rests on getting these three branches right and on knowing they are alternatives, not cumulative.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Marine casualty, marine incident, very serious marine casualty - how do they differ?
retrieval_cards.answer: A MARINE CASUALTY is an event, or sequence of events, resulting in any of seven consequences occurring directly in connection with the operations of a ship: death or serious injury; loss of a person from a ship; loss, presumed loss or abandonment of a ship; material damage to a ship; stranding, disabling or collision; material damage to marine infrastructure external to the ship that could seriously endanger safety; or severe damage to the environment or the potential for it. A MARINE INCIDENT is an event other than a marine casualty which endangered, or if not corrected would endanger, the safety of the ship, its occupants, any other person or the environment. A VERY SERIOUS MARINE CASUALTY is a subset of marine casualty - total loss, a death, or severe damage to the environment. NEITHER a marine casualty nor a marine incident includes a deliberate act or omission intended to cause harm.
retrieval_cards.why: The three sit inside each other and limb (c) cannot be answered for four marks without showing where the boundaries are. The deliberate-act exclusion is the detail most candidates miss.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is a marine safety investigation NOT for?
retrieval_cards.answer: It does not seek to apportion blame or determine liability. It is conducted with the objective of preventing marine casualties and marine incidents in the future, and should be separate from and independent of any other form of investigation, including investigations for civil, criminal and administrative proceedings. The Code is explicit that it is not intended to preclude other forms of investigation, and equally that a State should not refrain from fully reporting causal factors merely because blame or liability may be inferred from the findings.
retrieval_cards.why: The single most distinctive feature of the regime and the easiest mark in limb (b). The last clause is the one that shows real understanding.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Who must be told about a marine casualty, and by whom?
retrieval_cards.answer: On the high seas or in an exclusive economic zone, the flag State of the ship or ships involved notifies other substantially interested States as soon as reasonably practicable. Within the territory, including the territorial sea, of a coastal State, the flag State and the coastal State notify EACH OTHER and between them notify the other substantially interested States. Notification is not delayed for lack of complete information, and contains as much as is readily available of: the ship's name and flag State; the IMO ship identification number; the nature, location, time and date of the casualty; the number of seriously injured or killed; the consequences to individuals, property and the environment; and the identification of any other ship involved.
retrieval_cards.why: A compact, countable list that lifts limb (b) above generalities.

retrieval_cards.prompt: When is an investigation compulsory, and when must the report go to IMO?
retrieval_cards.answer: Chapter 6: a marine safety investigation SHALL be conducted into EVERY very serious marine casualty, and subject to any agreement under chapter 7 the flag State of a ship involved is responsible for ensuring it is conducted and completed in accordance with the Code. Chapter 14.1: the final version of the report SHALL be submitted to the Organization for every marine safety investigation conducted into a very serious marine casualty. Chapter 14.2: where an investigation into a lesser casualty or an incident produces a report containing information that may prevent or lessen the seriousness of future casualties, that final version shall also be submitted. Chapter 14.4: the final report is made available to the public and the shipping industry.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the payoff of limb (c) and it is what makes the classification worth four marks - VSMC is the trigger for both mandatory duties.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What protections does the Code give a seafarer whose evidence is taken?
retrieval_cards.answer: Chapter 12: evidence is taken at the earliest practical opportunity, and the seafarer is allowed to return to the ship or be repatriated at the earliest possible opportunity; the seafarer's human rights are upheld at all times. Every seafarer from whom evidence is sought is informed of the nature and basis of the investigation, and is informed of and allowed access to legal advice regarding any potential risk of self-incrimination in subsequent proceedings, any right not to self-incriminate or to remain silent, and any protections afforded to prevent the evidence being used against them. The regime sits alongside the Guidelines on Fair Treatment of Seafarers in the Event of a Maritime Accident, resolution A.987(24).
retrieval_cards.why: The human-element limb of the Code, and the part a Chief Engineer is most likely to meet in person. It is also the answer to 'why would anyone tell an investigator the truth?'
