blocks.h: 1. The Convention, and where the stem's facts have got to

blocks.p: The governing instrument is the International Convention on Salvage, 1989, which entered into force in 1996 and replaced the Brussels Convention of 1910. On the stem's facts a professional salvor has refloated a grounded ship and towed her to a place of safety. A useful result has therefore been achieved, which under article 12 is the condition of any payment at all - no cure, no pay, retained by the 1989 Convention rather than abolished by it. The entitlement has accrued, and the three limbs ask how it is quantified, what duties the parties owed one another while it was being earned, and what happens when the parties have also signed a contract.
MIW holds no licensed text of the Convention and no copy of LOF 2000 or SCOPIC. Articles and forms below are identified and described by effect; nothing is quoted, and no clause number is cited.

blocks.h: (a) The criteria under Article 13 for determining the amount of the award (6 marks)
2. The scheme Article 13 sits inside

blocks.p: Two articles work together and it is worth separating them in one line. Article 12 creates the entitlement: salvage operations which have had a useful result give right to a reward, and no payment is due if they have had no useful result. Article 13 then fixes the amount - and it does so, in the Convention's own words of purpose, with a view to encouraging salvage operations.

That phrase governs everything else in the limb. The reward is not a reimbursement of the salvor's costs, and it is not a quantum meruit for hours worked. It is deliberately set at a level intended to make it worth someone's while to own tugs, pumps and trained crews and keep them idle against the day they are needed. A candidate who explains that has explained why criterion (10) - the salvor's state of readiness and the value of his equipment - is in the list at all.

blocks.h: 3. The Article 13 criteria

blocks.p: The Convention lists ten. Give them all, and in this order, because the examiner has named the article:

ol: The salved value of the vessel and other property.
The skill and efforts of the salvors in preventing or minimising damage to the environment.
The measure of success obtained by the salvor.
The nature and degree of the danger.
The skill and efforts of the salvors in salving the vessel, other property and life.
The time used and the expenses and losses incurred by the salvors.
The risk of liability and other risks run by the salvors or their equipment.
The promptness of the services rendered.
The availability and use of vessels or other equipment intended for salvage operations.
The state of readiness and efficiency of the salvor's equipment and the value thereof.

blocks.p: Note where the environmental criterion sits. It is second, immediately after salved value - not appended at the end. That placement is the Convention's most important single reform: under the 1910 regime a salvor who spent days and money keeping oil off a coastline but saved nothing of value earned nothing for it, and the 1989 Convention rewards environmental protection inside the ordinary reward, before ever reaching the separate special compensation provisions.

blocks.h: 4. How the criteria are applied

ul: They are not in order of importance. The Convention says so expressly. All ten are weighed together in the round, and the relative weight depends on the casualty - danger and skill will dominate one case, promptness and readiness another.

The reward is capped. It shall not exceed the salved value of the vessel and other property. The salvor can never recover more than he saved, however heroic the operation or however great his expenditure.

The cap is why more was needed. Where the property saved is of little value but the environmental exposure is enormous - a laden tanker in ballast tanks aground on a coast - the cap can leave a salvor with a reward far below his costs. That is the gap the Convention's separate special compensation provisions were written to fill. Those are not the subject of this stem and are not developed here; they are mentioned so that the shape of the scheme is visible.

The criteria are applied by whoever fixes the award - by agreement between the parties, or failing that by the arbitrator or tribunal to whom the question has been referred. This is the point at which limb (a) hands over to limb (c).

blocks.h: 5. Who pays, and what can reduce or extinguish the award

blocks.p: Payment. The reward is payable by all of the vessel and other property interests in proportion to their respective salved values. Ship and cargo therefore contribute separately and proportionately - a point worth making, because it explains why a salvor takes security from cargo interests as well as from the owner before releasing the property, and why cargo underwriters are as interested in a salvage award as hull underwriters.
What reduces it. The scheme has teeth in both directions:

ul: Article 18 - a salvor may be deprived of the whole or part of the payment due to the extent that the salvage operations have become necessary or more difficult because of his own fault or neglect, or if he has been guilty of fraud or other dishonest conduct.

Article 19 - services rendered notwithstanding the express and reasonable prohibition of the owner or master of the vessel give rise to no payment under the Convention. A salvor cannot force his services on an unwilling ship and then present a bill.
And within article 13 itself, a poor measure of success, a lack of promptness or unimpressive skill and efforts simply produce a smaller award. The criteria cut both ways.

blocks.h: (b) The duties of the salvor and of the shipowner and master (5 marks)
6. The salvor's duties

blocks.p: Article 8 is the duties article and it is expressed as a reciprocal scheme. The salvor owes to the owner of the vessel or other property in danger a duty:

ol: to carry out the salvage operations with due care;
in performing that duty, to exercise due care to prevent or minimise damage to the environment;
whenever circumstances reasonably require, to seek assistance from other salvors; and

to accept the intervention of other salvors when reasonably requested to do so by the owner or master of the vessel - though the amount of his reward is not prejudiced should it be found that such a request was unreasonable.

blocks.p: Duties (3) and (4) are the ones candidates omit, and they are doing real work. A professional salvor who has a casualty under contract has an obvious commercial incentive to keep the job to himself; the Convention removes that incentive where the ship's interests require more resources than he has. The salvor may not hold a casualty hostage to his own capacity - and the closing qualification protects him from being displaced on an unreasonable demand.

blocks.h: 7. The duties of the owner and the master

blocks.p: The same article imposes duties the other way. The owner and master of the vessel or the owner of other property in danger owe the salvor a duty:

ol: to co-operate fully with him during the course of the salvage operations;
in doing so, to exercise due care to prevent or minimise damage to the environment; and
when the vessel or other property has been brought to a place of safety, to accept redelivery when reasonably requested by the salvor to do so.

blocks.p: The third duty fits the stem's facts exactly. The examiner has told you the ship has been towed by the salvor to a place of safety - which is precisely the trigger for the owner's obligation to take her back when reasonably asked. It exists because the alternative is a salvor left holding a damaged ship he cannot dispose of and cannot leave, accruing cost, while the owner delays redelivery to improve his negotiating position on security.

blocks.h: 8. The mutual character of the duties, the master's authority, and breach

ul: The environmental duty is imposed on both sides, and that is the Convention's genuine innovation. The 1910 regime asked only whether property had been saved. The 1989 Convention makes the prevention of environmental damage a duty of the owner and master as well as of the salvor, rewards it in the article 13 criteria, and backs it with separate compensation provisions. An answer that gives the environmental duty only to the salvor has given half of it.

The master's authority to contract. Under article 6 the master has authority to conclude contracts for salvage operations on behalf of the owner of the vessel, and the master or the owner has authority to conclude such contracts on behalf of the owner of the property on board. This is the provision that makes limb (c) possible at all: it is why a form can be signed at three in the morning by the only person present with authority, without waiting for owners, charterers, cargo interests and underwriters to be assembled.

Breach. The Convention does not create a tariff of penalties for breach of article 8. Its consequences run through the rest of the scheme: a salvor whose want of due care made the operation necessary or more difficult may be deprived of all or part of his reward under article 18; an owner or master who fails to co-operate, or who refuses reasonable redelivery, exposes himself to liability for the loss that follows and weakens his position on the assessment; and failure by either side to exercise due care for the environment bears directly on the article 13 assessment and on the special compensation provisions.

blocks.h: (c) LOF 2000 - when the Convention applies, and when the LOF (5 marks)
9. What LOF 2000 is, and what it is not

blocks.p: Lloyd's Open Form is a standard-form salvage contract. It is commercial contract, not an international instrument, and the single most common error on this limb is to treat it as though it competed with the Convention on the same plane. Its defining characteristics are:

ul: It is 'open' - the remuneration is deliberately not fixed at the time of agreement. That is the whole point of the form: at a casualty nobody can price the job, so the parties agree that it will be done and that the price will be settled afterwards.
It is no cure, no pay, mirroring the Convention's own condition of payment.

It is short and can be agreed in minutes, often verbally and confirmed later, and typically signed by the master under his article 6 authority - which is why work can begin while the ship is still in danger.
It fixes the machinery, not the amount - who will determine the sum, under what law, where, and how the property will be secured in the meantime.

blocks.p: SCOPIC is a separate contractual supplement which the parties may incorporate, providing an alternative, tariff-based method of remunerating a salvor in circumstances where the ordinary reward may be inadequate. It too is industry contract, outside the Convention. No clause of either the LOF or SCOPIC is quoted or cited here.

blocks.h: 10. When the Convention applies

blocks.p: The Convention applies as the general law of salvage in any State that has given it effect, and it governs by default. Its own article 6 sets out the relationship with contracts:

ul: The Convention applies to any salvage operation save to the extent that a contract otherwise provides, expressly or by implication. Parties are therefore free to vary its terms by agreement, and an LOF is exactly such an agreement.
But the freedom is not unlimited. The duties in article 8 - including the environmental duties on both sides - cannot be contracted out of.

And the Convention supervises the bargain. A contract or any of its terms may be annulled or modified where the contract has been entered into under undue influence or the influence of danger and its terms are inequitable, or where the payment under the contract is in an excessive degree too large or too small for the services actually rendered.

blocks.p: That supervisory power is the answer to the obvious objection to signing anything in an emergency. A master agreeing terms with a ship aground and making water is, by definition, not negotiating freely, and the Convention accordingly reserves the right to reopen a bargain struck in those conditions.

blocks.h: 11. When the LOF applies

blocks.p: Where the parties have agreed an LOF, its terms govern the relationship between them to the extent that they provide for the matter in hand. In practice the form governs:

ul: the fact and scope of the engagement - that the salvor will use best endeavours to salve the property and take it to an agreed or a place of safety;

the forum and the law - that the amount of any award, and any dispute, will be referred to arbitration in London under the terms of the form and the law it specifies, rather than to a court in whatever jurisdiction the casualty happens to lie;
security - the obligation on the property interests to provide security for the salvor's claim, and the salvor's corresponding obligation to release the property once it is given; and
the procedure - the appointment of the arbitrator, the appeal structure within the form, and the administration of the reference.

blocks.p: What the LOF does not do is create the entitlement or supply the criteria. It records that a reward will be payable if the operation succeeds and provides the machinery for fixing it; the substantive principles the arbitrator applies are the Convention's.

blocks.h: 12. How a dispute is actually resolved under an LOF

ol: The ship is salved and delivered to a place of safety. Security is provided by the ship and cargo interests, on the form's terms, and the property is released - which is what allows the ship to trade and the cargo to move while the money is argued about.

The salvor's claim is referred to arbitration in London in accordance with the form. This is the practical significance of the LOF and it is where most of the marks in limb (c) are: the form has removed the question of forum from the dispute entirely. There is no argument about which country's courts have jurisdiction, no race to arrest, and no forum-shopping - a real gain when a casualty may involve a ship of one flag, a salvor of another, cargo owned in a third and a coastline belonging to a fourth.

The arbitrator fixes the amount by applying the Article 13 criteria - salved value, environmental efforts, measure of success, danger, skill, time and expense, risks run, promptness, availability and readiness - and observes the cap at salved value, apportioning the liability between ship and cargo in proportion to their salved values.
An appeal lies within the structure the form itself provides, and the award is then enforceable against the security already held.

blocks.h: 13. The relationship, stated as a rule

rows: Nature
International instrument, given effect in national law
Commercial contract between the parties
Supplies
The substantive law - entitlement, criteria, duties, cap, apportionment, and the grounds for reopening a bargain
The machinery - engagement, forum, governing law, security, arbitration and appeal
Applies
By default, to any salvage operation, save to the extent a contract otherwise provides
By agreement, and only between the parties who agreed it
Can be displaced
Only in part. The article 8 duties cannot be contracted out of, and an inequitable or grossly mispriced contract may be annulled or modified
Entirely - the parties need not use it, and may agree different terms
If the two conflict
The Convention prevails where the contract would defeat its protective provisions
Governs where it validly provides for the matter

blocks.p: The rule to write down is short: the contract governs procedure and terms; the Convention governs substance; where the contract is silent the Convention fills the gap; and where the contract would defeat the Convention's protective provisions, the Convention prevails.

blocks.h: 14. Why the arrangement exists at all

blocks.p: Close by explaining why two documents are needed rather than one, because it makes the whole answer cohere.

A casualty demands a decision in minutes and a valuation that takes months. Nobody at the scene knows how long the work will take, what it will cost, whether it will succeed, or what the property will be worth when it is safe. So the two functions are split. The form lets the work start at once, on terms brief enough for a master to accept while his ship is still aground, and settles in advance the questions that would otherwise be fought over afterwards - who decides, under what law, where, and against what security. The Convention then supplies the principles on which the sum is fixed, guarantees the duties neither side may bargain away, protects the party who agreed terms under the influence of danger, and rewards the salvor for protecting a coastline whose owner is not a party to anything.

Between them they answer the question that makes professional salvage possible: why would anyone sail towards a ship that nobody has yet agreed to pay for? Because success is rewarded on principled criteria that recognise readiness and risk as well as effort; because failure genuinely earns nothing, which keeps the industry honest; and because the terms on which all of that will be decided were settled before anyone had time to argue.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: The printed marks are 6 / 5 / 5 and the limbs are three different tasks. Limb (a) says list, so it must be a numbered list - the examiner has named Article 13, which means partial recall of the criteria will be visible as partial recall. Give all ten. Limb (b) is two-sided and the second side is where the marks hide. Limb (c) is the limb most candidates lose, and it is worth as much as limb (b).

Spend your time in proportion. A common failure is a beautiful limb (a) followed by two thin paragraphs - because the criteria are memorable and the duties and the contract are not. If you are short of time, a bare list of the ten criteria takes ninety seconds and then limb (c) deserves the rest.

In limb (c), the sentence that earns the most is the one that says what each document actually does: the contract fixes forum, law, security and machinery; the Convention supplies the criteria the arbitrator applies. Everything else in that limb is elaboration of that sentence.

blocks.h: The idea underneath salvage law

blocks.p: Salvage exists because ordinary contract law cannot do the job. Normally you agree a price and then do the work. At a casualty that is impossible in both directions: the salvor cannot price a job whose duration, difficulty and outcome are unknown, and the owner cannot negotiate freely with a ship aground and making water. If the law required a bargain, either nothing would happen or everything would be extortion.

So the law substitutes a different arrangement: do the work, and if it succeeds you will be paid an amount fixed afterwards on settled criteria. That single move solves both problems. The salvor does not need a price to start. The owner cannot be held to ransom, because the amount will be assessed rather than demanded. And because the assessment expressly aims to encourage salvage operations, it can be generous enough to sustain an industry that must keep expensive equipment idle most of the time - which is why readiness and the value of the salvor's equipment are among the criteria, and why 'you only worked for two days' is not an answer to a large award.

The 1989 Convention then adds the piece the 1910 regime lacked. Under the old law a salvor was rewarded for saving property, so a tanker that could not be saved but whose oil could be kept off a coastline earned him precisely nothing - which meant the law was paying salvors to make exactly the wrong choice about where to put their effort. The 1989 Convention rewards environmental protection inside the ordinary reward criteria, imposes environmental duties on both parties, and provides separately for the case where the property saved is too small to fund the effort. Understand that one reform and most of the Convention's shape follows.

blocks.h: The criteria - how to remember all ten

blocks.p: They fall into four groups, and grouped they are much easier to reproduce under pressure.

rows: What was at stake
Salved value; nature and degree of the danger
What the salvor achieved
Skill and efforts in preventing or minimising environmental damage; measure of success; skill and efforts in salving vessel, property and life
What it cost him
Time used, expenses and losses incurred; risk of liability and other risks run
How well he was placed to do it
Promptness; availability and use of vessels and equipment; state of readiness, efficiency and value of the equipment

blocks.p: The last group is the one people forget and it is the most interesting. It rewards the salvor for things that happened before the casualty - for having bought the tugs, maintained them and had them where they were needed. That is the law deliberately paying for standing capacity, and it is the clearest evidence that the award is not a fee for hours worked.

blocks.h: Article 8 - the duties, and the half everyone misses

blocks.p: Almost every candidate can say the salvor must exercise due care. Rather fewer say he must seek assistance from other salvors when circumstances reasonably require and accept their intervention when reasonably requested by the owner or master. Fewer still give the duties on the other side at all.
Learn the reciprocal shape:

rows: Carry out the operations with due care
Co-operate fully with him during the operations
Exercise due care to prevent or minimise damage to the environment
Exercise due care to prevent or minimise damage to the environment
Seek assistance from other salvors when circumstances reasonably require
Accept the intervention of other salvors when reasonably requested by the owner or master
Accept redelivery when the property is brought to a place of safety and he is reasonably requested to do so

blocks.p: Note the symmetry of the middle row - identical wording, both sides - and note that the two bottom-row duties are each about not obstructing the other party's legitimate interest. That is the design: neither side may use the emergency as leverage.

blocks.h: LOF and the Convention - the mistake to avoid

blocks.p: The commonest error in limb (c) is to write as though the question were 'which of these two applies?', as if they were rival sources of law competing for the same territory. They are not. One is a treaty and one is a contract, and they operate on different questions.

Think of it as a division of labour. The Convention answers: is a reward payable at all? on what criteria? capped at what? paid by whom? what duties did each party owe? and can this bargain be reopened? The LOF answers: are we agreed that you will start work? who will decide the amount? under what law? where? and how is the property secured in the meantime?

Once you see that, the exceptions make sense too. The Convention lets the parties vary its terms by contract - because most of it is default machinery. But it will not let them contract out of the article 8 duties, and it reserves power to annul or modify a contract made under the influence of danger on inequitable terms, or one where the payment is in an excessive degree too large or too small. Those are the protective provisions, and they are the answer to 'what if the master signs something disastrous?'

blocks.h: Why arbitration in London matters more than it sounds

blocks.p: It is easy to read 'arbitration in London under English law' as a piece of parochial detail. It is not. Consider the alternative on a real casualty: a ship of one flag, salvors of another nationality, cargo owned in several countries, insurers in more, and a grounding on the coast of a State with its own interest in the outcome. Without an agreed forum, the first dispute is about where the dispute will be heard, and the salvor's practical remedy is to arrest the property wherever he can reach it.

The form removes all of that in advance, before anyone knows whether there will be an argument. The greatest practical value of the LOF is not what it says about money; it is that it settles the questions that would otherwise be fought over first. That, plus the security provisions that let the ship trade and the cargo move while the amount is assessed, is what makes the form worth signing.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: Answering on Article 14 special compensation. This stem does not ask for it. Mention it in one clause to explain why the salved-value cap needed a companion provision, and move on - a full treatment is the answer to a different question.
Treating LOF 2000 as an instrument. It is a contract. Say so.
Quoting an LOF or SCOPIC clause number. Both forms exist in several editions and clause numbering differs. Describe by function.
Giving only the salvor's duties. Article 8 is reciprocal, and the owner's duty to accept redelivery fits the stem's facts exactly.
Saying the criteria are in order of importance. The Convention says they are not.
Forgetting the cap and the apportionment. The reward cannot exceed the salved value and is paid by ship and cargo in proportion to their salved values - two easy marks.
Saying no cure no pay was abolished in 1989. It was retained. What was added was a way of paying for environmental effort when the property saved could not fund it.
Reaching for the Merchant Shipping Act 2025. It commenced 15 March 2026, nineteen months after this sitting - and the stem asks about the Convention in any event.

blocks.h: If you only have ten minutes for this question

blocks.p: (a), six lines. Under the Salvage Convention 1989, article 12 gives the right to a reward where the operation has had a useful result - no cure, no pay - and article 13 fixes the amount, with a view to encouraging salvage operations. The criteria are: salved value of the vessel and other property; skill and efforts in preventing or minimising damage to the environment; measure of success; nature and degree of the danger; skill and efforts in salving the vessel, other property and life; time used and expenses and losses incurred; risk of liability and other risks run; promptness of the services; availability and use of vessels or other equipment intended for salvage; and the state of readiness, efficiency and value of the salvor's equipment. They are not in order of importance; the reward cannot exceed the salved value; and it is paid by ship and cargo in proportion to their salved values. Article 18 may deprive a salvor of all or part for his own fault or dishonesty, and article 19 denies payment for services rendered against express and reasonable prohibition.

(b), four lines. Article 8 imposes duties on both sides. The salvor must carry out the operations with due care; in doing so exercise due care to prevent or minimise damage to the environment; seek assistance from other salvors whenever circumstances reasonably require; and accept their intervention when reasonably requested by the owner or master, without prejudice to his reward if the request proves unreasonable. The owner and master must co-operate fully with the salvor; in doing so exercise due care to prevent or minimise damage to the environment; and, when the property has been brought to a place of safety, accept redelivery when reasonably requested. Note that under article 6 the master has authority to conclude a salvage contract on behalf of the owner.

(c), five lines. LOF 2000 is Lloyd's Open Form - a standard-form salvage contract, not an instrument: no cure no pay, remuneration deliberately left open, signable in minutes by the master. The Convention applies as the general law and governs by default; article 6 provides that it applies to any salvage operation save to the extent a contract otherwise provides, but the article 8 duties cannot be contracted out of and a contract made under the influence of danger on inequitable terms, or grossly mispriced, may be annulled or modified. The LOF applies between the parties who agreed it and fixes the machinery: the engagement, security for the claim and release of the property, and reference of the amount and of any dispute to arbitration in London under the form's terms and law, with its own appeal structure. In a dispute, therefore, the LOF determines where, under what law and by whom the question is decided, while the arbitrator applies the Convention's Article 13 criteria to fix the sum. The rule: the contract governs procedure and terms, the Convention governs substance, and where the contract would defeat the Convention's protective provisions the Convention prevails.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

blocks.p: These are the places this particular question goes wrong, taken from the ambiguities identified before drafting and from the single error most likely to cost marks.

The one that costs most: Treating LOF 2000 as though it were a legal instrument that competes with the Convention. It is a standard-form CONTRACT. It fixes the forum, the governing law, the security arrangements and the machinery for fixing the sum; the CONVENTION supplies the substantive principles the arbitrator applies. The second trap is forgetting that Article 8 imposes duties on the SHIPOWNER AND MASTER as well as on the salvor - including the duty to ACCEPT REDELIVERY - which is half of limb (b). The third is answering on Article 14 special compensation, which this stem does not ask for.
The wording of the stem invites four specific misreadings, and each is resolved in the answer rather than left to chance:

ul: Limb (c) as printed - 'discuss when the Convention is applicable and when the LOF if any dispute arises' - is grammatically incomplete and could be read two ways: when does each of the two GOVERN, or which forum resolves the dispute. The answer takes it as BOTH, because the two readings are complementary and each carries marks: it explains the substantive division between Convention and contract, and then explains the arbitration machinery. Reproduced as printed and answered on both readings.

The stem says the salvor 'has a right to award'. Strictly the right arises under article 12 from the useful result, and article 13 quantifies it. The answer says so in one line without labouring it, because the stem has plainly given success as a fact.

'Duties of the salvor and the shipowner/master' - the printed pairing invites treating owner and master as one. Their duties largely coincide under article 8, but the MASTER additionally has authority to conclude a salvage contract on behalf of the owner. The answer notes that separately because it is the practical link to limb (c).

Article 14 special compensation is NOT asked. It is referred to only so far as is needed to explain why the article 13 cap makes some such provision necessary, and is not developed. Answering the donor's question instead of this one would be the most likely way to waste time here.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

blocks.p: The retrieval questions below are the ones this answer is built to survive. They are the same questions an examiner reaches for when testing whether a written answer was understood or reproduced.

ul: Give the route for the salvage award, duties and LOF question. — Printed 6/5/5. Limb (a) says LIST, so number the criteria; limb (c) is the limb candidates lose and it needs five short sections, not one paragraph.

List the Article 13 criteria for fixing the salvage reward. — Six marks and the examiner named the article, so a selection reads as partial recall. Give all ten in the Convention's own order - and note that the ENVIRONMENTAL criterion sits second, not last.
How are the Article 13 criteria applied? — Two of the six marks in limb (a) are here rather than in the list itself, and the 'encouraging salvage operations' point explains the whole design.

What are the salvor's duties under the Convention? — Half of limb (b). The duty to accept another salvor's intervention is the one candidates never give, and it is the provision that stops a salvor holding a casualty hostage.

What are the duties of the owner and master of the vessel in danger? — The other half of limb (b), and the half most often omitted. Note how directly it fits the stem's facts: the ship HAS been towed to a place of safety, so the redelivery duty is live.
LOF 2000 or the Convention - which governs what? — The whole of limb (c) in one card, and the point that separates a good answer from a vague one.

When does the Convention apply, and can the parties contract out of it? — 'When is the Convention applicable' is answered here, and the protective provisions are what stop a distressed master signing away everything.
What can reduce or extinguish a salvor's award? — Rounds out limb (a) and shows the scheme has teeth on both sides - the salvor is not merely a beneficiary of it.

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: The route, chunked: SCENE (1). (a) FOUR: THE SCHEME (2), THE LIST (3), HOW APPLIED (4), WHO PAYS (5). (b) THREE: SALVOR (6), OWNER AND MASTER (7), MUTUAL AND BREACH (8). (c) FIVE: WHAT LOF IS (9), CONVENTION WHEN (10), LOF WHEN (11), THE DISPUTE (12), THE RULE (13). CLOSE: WHY (14).

Fifteen-second recall: Salvage Convention 1989, in force 1996, replaced the 1910 Convention; retains NO CURE NO PAY (article 12 - a useful result). Article 13 criteria, unranked: salved value; skill and efforts in preventing or minimising damage to the environment; measure of success; nature and degree of danger; skill and efforts in salving the vessel, other property and life; time used and expenses and losses incurred; risk of liability and other risks run; promptness; availability and use of vessels or other equipment; and the state of readiness, efficiency and value of the salvor's equipment. Reward CAPPED at salved value; paid by ship and cargo in PROPORTION to their salved values. Article 8 duties, BOTH SIDES: the salvor must use due care, prevent or minimise environmental damage, seek other salvors when reasonably required and accept their intervention when reasonably requested; the owner and master must co-operate fully, exercise due care for the environment, and ACCEPT REDELIVERY when brought to a place of safety and reasonably requested. LOF 2000 is a CONTRACT, not an instrument: no cure no pay, signed in minutes, arbitration in London under English law, security given before release; the Convention supplies the substantive criteria the arbitrator applies.
The numbers and thresholds worth carrying exactly:

decomposition_gate.question_intent: A scenario stem followed by three printed limbs at 6, 5 and 5. The scenario matters: a grounded ship has been REFLOATED and TOWED TO A PLACE OF SAFETY by a PROFESSIONAL SALVOR, and the stem states that the salvor has a right to award. That is a deliberate framing - success has been achieved, so the entitlement question is settled and the examiner is asking about QUANTIFICATION, DUTIES and the CONTRACT. Limb (a) is a LIST question and must be answered as an enumerated list. Limb (b) is a two-sided duties question. Limb (c) is the discriminating limb and the least well answered: when does the Convention govern and when does the LOF, if a dispute arises.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 6 + 5 + 5, printed. In limb (a), roughly four marks for the criteria themselves - given in full and in the Convention's own order - and two for how they are applied: unranked, capped at salved value, and payable by the interests in proportion. In limb (b), roughly two and a half marks for the salvor's duties and two and a half for the owner's and master's, with the mutual environmental duty worth explicit mention on both sides. In limb (c), roughly one mark for what LOF 2000 is, two for the Convention/contract division, and two for how a dispute is actually resolved - arbitration, the applicable law and the security.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That the candidate can give the Article 13 criteria substantially in full, knows they are UNRANKED, knows the reward is capped at salved value and paid by ship and cargo in proportion, and knows the environmental criterion appears in Article 13 as well as in Article 14. On duties, that the candidate knows the Convention imposes duties on BOTH sides and that the duty to prevent or minimise environmental damage falls on the owner and master as well as on the salvor - which is the Convention's genuine innovation and the point most often missed. On limb (c), that the candidate can separate the CONTRACT, which fixes forum, law, security and machinery, from the CONVENTION, which supplies the substantive criteria - and does not describe the LOF as though it were a treaty.
primary_source_plan: Establish FIRST that MIW holds no copy of the Convention and no copy of LOF 2000 or SCOPIC, and resolve to cite by identity only and to quote nothing - on a treaty question with no held text the danger is invented article numbers, and on a contract question it is invented clause numbers
Read the donor QP2411-Q5 in full and adopt its evidence discipline together with its Article 13 content
Read QP2406-Q8, which pre-dates this sitting by two months, for the house position on the principles of modern salvage law, so this answer does not contradict it
Carry the Article 13 criteria in the Convention's own order, with the environmental criterion in its correct position
Build limb (b) around article 8, which the donor does not address, and state the duties as the two-sided scheme they are
Build limb (c) around article 6 and the division between contract and Convention, being careful to describe the LOF by function and not by clause
State the evidence gap in the answer itself, not only in the metadata
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: LOW on the treaty, which is unamended and has been in force since 1996 - there is no edition question and no amendment to track. MEDIUM on the surrounding CONTRACTUAL layer: LOF and SCOPIC have both been revised more than once, so any edition year asserted would be a currency exposure. That is controlled by naming no edition other than the LOF 2000 the stem itself supplies, by citing no clause number, and by classifying both expressly as industry contract outside the Convention.

questions.understand_first: A ship is aground and there is no time. Somebody with tugs and pumps and people who know what they are doing has to decide, now, whether to sail towards her - and the owner has to decide, now, whether to let them. Neither side can possibly agree a price at that moment: nobody knows how long it will take, what it will cost, whether it will work, or what the ship and her cargo will turn out to be worth when she is safe. So the law does something unusual. It says: go and do the work, and if you succeed you will be paid, and the amount will be worked out afterwards by someone applying settled criteria. If you fail, you get nothing. That single arrangement - reward for success, nothing for failure - is what makes a professional salvage industry possible, because it turns an act of rescue into a business that can own expensive equipment and keep it waiting. The rest follows from it. Because the reward is fixed afterwards, there has to be a list of things the person fixing it must weigh - how dangerous it was, how skilful, how quick, what was risked, and what was saved. Because a rescuer who is paid only for saving property has no reason to care about oil on a beach, the list was expanded to reward protecting the coastline too, and duties to look after the environment were placed on both sides - the salvor and the shipowner. And because none of this can be negotiated line by line on a lee shore, the industry uses a short standard form that the master can sign in minutes, which settles who decides the amount, under what law, and where - while leaving the amount itself to be worked out later on the settled criteria. So the two documents in this question are not rivals. One says what a rescue is worth; the other is how you get started before anyone has time to argue about it.
questions.memory_cue: SCENE (1). (a) FOUR: THE SCHEME (2), THE LIST (3), HOW APPLIED (4), WHO PAYS (5). (b) THREE: SALVOR (6), OWNER AND MASTER (7), MUTUAL AND BREACH (8). (c) FIVE: WHAT LOF IS (9), CONVENTION WHEN (10), LOF WHEN (11), THE DISPUTE (12), THE RULE (13). CLOSE: WHY (14).

quick_revision.recall_15s: Salvage Convention 1989, in force 1996, replaced the 1910 Convention; retains NO CURE NO PAY (article 12 - a useful result). Article 13 criteria, unranked: salved value; skill and efforts in preventing or minimising damage to the environment; measure of success; nature and degree of danger; skill and efforts in salving the vessel, other property and life; time used and expenses and losses incurred; risk of liability and other risks run; promptness; availability and use of vessels or other equipment; and the state of readiness, efficiency and value of the salvor's equipment. Reward CAPPED at salved value; paid by ship and cargo in PROPORTION to their salved values. Article 8 duties, BOTH SIDES: the salvor must use due care, prevent or minimise environmental damage, seek other salvors when reasonably required and accept their intervention when reasonably requested; the owner and master must co-operate fully, exercise due care for the environment, and ACCEPT REDELIVERY when brought to a place of safety and reasonably requested. LOF 2000 is a CONTRACT, not an instrument: no cure no pay, signed in minutes, arbitration in London under English law, security given before release; the Convention supplies the substantive criteria the arbitrator applies.
critical_numbers: International Convention on Salvage, 1989 - in force 1996; replaced the Brussels Convention of 1910
Article 12 - the condition of payment: no payment is due unless the operation has had a useful result
Article 13 - TEN criteria for fixing the reward, and they are NOT in order of importance
The reward shall NOT EXCEED the salved value of the vessel and other property
Payable by the vessel and other property interests IN PROPORTION to their respective salved values
Article 8 - duties on BOTH the salvor and the owner and master
Article 14 - special compensation; not the subject of this stem, referred to only as part of the scheme
NO ARTICLE IS QUOTED AND NO LOF CLAUSE IS CITED - MIW holds neither text
quick_revision.critical_regulation: International Convention on Salvage, 1989 - articles 6, 8, 12 and 13 in particular; with LOF 2000 and SCOPIC identified as COMMERCIAL CONTRACT outside the Convention.
quick_revision.major_trap: Treating LOF 2000 as though it were a legal instrument that competes with the Convention. It is a standard-form CONTRACT. It fixes the forum, the governing law, the security arrangements and the machinery for fixing the sum; the CONVENTION supplies the substantive principles the arbitrator applies. The second trap is forgetting that Article 8 imposes duties on the SHIPOWNER AND MASTER as well as on the salvor - including the duty to ACCEPT REDELIVERY - which is half of limb (b). The third is answering on Article 14 special compensation, which this stem does not ask for.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the salvage award, duties and LOF question.
retrieval_cards.answer: Scene: 1 the Convention and the facts. (a) 2 the scheme - no cure no pay under article 12, reward under article 13. 3 the ten criteria. 4 how they are applied - unranked and capped. 5 who pays and what reduces the award. (b) 6 the salvor's duties. 7 the owner's and master's duties. 8 the mutual environmental duty and breach. (c) 9 what LOF 2000 is. 10 when the Convention applies. 11 when the LOF applies. 12 how a dispute is resolved. 13 the relationship stated as a rule. 14 why the arrangement exists.
retrieval_cards.why: Printed 6/5/5. Limb (a) says LIST, so number the criteria; limb (c) is the limb candidates lose and it needs five short sections, not one paragraph.

retrieval_cards.prompt: List the Article 13 criteria for fixing the salvage reward.
retrieval_cards.answer: (1) The salved value of the vessel and other property. (2) The skill and efforts of the salvors in preventing or minimising damage to the environment. (3) The measure of success obtained by the salvor. (4) The nature and degree of the danger. (5) The skill and efforts of the salvors in salving the vessel, other property and life. (6) The time used and the expenses and losses incurred by the salvors. (7) The risk of liability and other risks run by the salvors or their equipment. (8) The promptness of the services rendered. (9) The availability and use of vessels or other equipment intended for salvage operations. (10) The state of readiness and efficiency of the salvor's equipment and the value thereof.
retrieval_cards.why: Six marks and the examiner named the article, so a selection reads as partial recall. Give all ten in the Convention's own order - and note that the ENVIRONMENTAL criterion sits second, not last.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How are the Article 13 criteria applied?
retrieval_cards.answer: They are NOT set out in order of importance and are taken together, all of them weighed in the round by whoever fixes the award. The reward is FIXED WITH A VIEW TO ENCOURAGING SALVAGE OPERATIONS - so it is not merely a reimbursement of cost, and a salvor who does an outstanding job on a difficult casualty is meant to do well out of it. The reward SHALL NOT EXCEED the salved value of the vessel and other property, and it is payable by the vessel and other property interests IN PROPORTION to their respective salved values.
retrieval_cards.why: Two of the six marks in limb (a) are here rather than in the list itself, and the 'encouraging salvage operations' point explains the whole design.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the salvor's duties under the Convention?
retrieval_cards.answer: Article 8. The salvor owes a duty to the owner of the vessel or other property in danger: to carry out the salvage operations WITH DUE CARE; in performing that duty, to exercise DUE CARE TO PREVENT OR MINIMISE DAMAGE TO THE ENVIRONMENT; whenever circumstances reasonably require, to SEEK ASSISTANCE FROM OTHER SALVORS; and to ACCEPT THE INTERVENTION OF OTHER SALVORS when reasonably requested to do so by the owner or master of the vessel - though the amount of his reward is not prejudiced should it be found that such a request was unreasonable.
retrieval_cards.why: Half of limb (b). The duty to accept another salvor's intervention is the one candidates never give, and it is the provision that stops a salvor holding a casualty hostage.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the duties of the owner and master of the vessel in danger?
retrieval_cards.answer: Article 8 again, and this is the Convention's innovation. The owner and master owe a duty to the salvor: to CO-OPERATE FULLY with him during the course of the operations; in doing so, to exercise DUE CARE TO PREVENT OR MINIMISE DAMAGE TO THE ENVIRONMENT; and, when the vessel or other property has been brought to a PLACE OF SAFETY, to ACCEPT REDELIVERY when reasonably requested by the salvor to do so.
retrieval_cards.why: The other half of limb (b), and the half most often omitted. Note how directly it fits the stem's facts: the ship HAS been towed to a place of safety, so the redelivery duty is live.

retrieval_cards.prompt: LOF 2000 or the Convention - which governs what?
retrieval_cards.answer: THE CONTRACT GOVERNS PROCEDURE AND TERMS; THE CONVENTION GOVERNS THE SUBSTANCE. LOF 2000 is a standard-form salvage CONTRACT - it can be agreed in minutes, often by the master under his article 6 authority, on a no cure no pay basis with the remuneration left to be fixed later. What it fixes is the machinery: that the amount will be determined by ARBITRATION in London under the terms of the form and the law it specifies; how SECURITY is to be provided before the property is released; and the appeal structure. What it does NOT do is create the entitlement or supply the criteria - those come from the Convention, and the arbitrator applies the Article 13 criteria.
retrieval_cards.why: The whole of limb (c) in one card, and the point that separates a good answer from a vague one.

retrieval_cards.prompt: When does the Convention apply, and can the parties contract out of it?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Convention applies as the general law of salvage wherever a State has given it effect, and it governs by default. Article 6 provides that the Convention applies to any salvage operation SAVE TO THE EXTENT THAT A CONTRACT OTHERWISE PROVIDES, EXPRESSLY OR BY IMPLICATION - so parties may vary its terms by agreement, and an LOF is exactly such an agreement. BUT the freedom is not unlimited: the duties in article 8 - including the environmental duties - cannot be contracted out of, and a contract or its terms may be annulled or modified where it was entered into under undue influence or the influence of danger and its terms are inequitable, or where the payment is in an excessive degree too large or too small for the services actually rendered.
retrieval_cards.why: 'When is the Convention applicable' is answered here, and the protective provisions are what stop a distressed master signing away everything.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What can reduce or extinguish a salvor's award?
retrieval_cards.answer: Article 18 - a salvor may be DEPRIVED OF THE WHOLE OR PART of the payment due where the salvage operations have become necessary or more difficult BECAUSE OF HIS OWN FAULT OR NEGLECT, or where he has been guilty of fraud or other dishonest conduct. Article 19 - services rendered NOTWITHSTANDING THE EXPRESS AND REASONABLE PROHIBITION of the owner or master of the vessel give rise to no payment under the Convention. And under article 13 itself, a poor measure of success or a lack of promptness simply produces a smaller award.
retrieval_cards.why: Rounds out limb (a) and shows the scheme has teeth on both sides - the salvor is not merely a beneficiary of it.

blocks.h: 1. Why the turbocharger is where the gains now are

blocks.p: Of the energy in the fuel, only about a third leaves a large marine diesel engine as work at the coupling. The single largest remaining share leaves as exhaust gas - hot, and at pressure. For most of the history of turbocharging, the whole of the useful part of that stream was needed for one job: driving the compressor that supplies the engine's air.

That is no longer true at the top of the load range. Turbocharger efficiency has risen to the point where the turbine can extract more energy than the compressor requires, and the difference is a genuine, continuously available surplus that used to be thrown away. All three devices in this question are ways of putting that surplus - or, in one case, its absence - to use.

blocks.h: 2. The common thread, and the division that organises the answer

blocks.p: Each device places an electrical machine somewhere in the exhaust energy path. What separates them is where the machine sits and which way the energy flows.

headers: Load range where it earns its keep

blocks.p: Harvest at high load; supply at low load. Keep that division in view and the three notes below arrange themselves.

blocks.h: (a) Power turbine generators (6 marks)
3. What it is

blocks.p: A power turbine generator is a separate exhaust gas turbine, additional to and independent of the turbocharger, fed by a portion of the exhaust gas bypassed around the turbocharger through a control valve. The turbine drives an electrical generator, normally through reduction gearing, because the turbine runs at a speed far above that of any practicable generator.

The essential point of identification is that this is an additional machine, not a modification of the turbocharger. The turbocharger continues to do its own job on the gas that is not bypassed; the power turbine works on the surplus.

blocks.h: 4. How it is arranged and controlled

ul: The gas path. A bypass line and control valve take gas from upstream of the turbocharger turbine and pass it to the power turbine, whose exhaust rejoins the main uptake. The valve position is the principal control: it determines how much energy is diverted, and it must never divert so much that the turbocharger is starved and the engine loses scavenge pressure.
The mechanical path. Power turbine, reduction gearing, and often a clutch or coupling allowing the machine to be disengaged when it is not in use.

The electrical path. The generator is synchronised with the ship's electrical system so that its output displaces auxiliary generator load, allowing one or more auxiliary engines to be unloaded or stopped.

Engagement. The machine is engaged only above the engine load at which a surplus actually exists. Below that it is bypassed or declutched, because taking gas from the turbocharger at low load would make the engine's air supply worse, not better.

Variants. Installations genuinely differ. Some recover the energy into the propulsion shaft line through a shaft motor or gearing rather than into a generator; some combine the power turbine with a steam turbine driven by an exhaust gas boiler in a combined recovery plant feeding a single generator. The answer should note the alternatives rather than present one as universal.

blocks.h: 5. What it buys, and what it costs

rows: Electrical power produced without additional fuel - the ship's service load is met from energy that was previously wasted
No benefit below a threshold load. On a ship that slow-steams, manoeuvres frequently or spends long periods at anchor, the machine may be engaged for a small fraction of her time
Auxiliary generator engines can be unloaded or stopped, saving their fuel, their running hours, their lubricating oil and their maintenance
Capital cost, weight and space - a turbine, gearing, a generator, a bypass valve and its control, and the switchboard interface

Improves the ship's energy efficiency in the form the regulation measures it - the attained design index and the operational carbon intensity both improve, because less fuel is burned for the same transport work
Complexity and new failure modes - the bypass valve, the gearing and its lubrication, and a high-speed machine in a hot gas stream
It does not touch the combustion process, so it does not disturb the engine's certified NOx configuration
It takes gas from the turbocharger. Control must protect the engine's air supply as the first priority, and a bypass valve failure is an engine problem, not merely a lost-generation problem

blocks.h: (b) Hybrid turbochargers (5 marks)
6. What it is

blocks.p: A hybrid turbocharger integrates an electrical machine onto the turbocharger's own shaft, so that the assembly which compresses the engine's air can also exchange electrical power with the ship. There is no separate turbine and no bypass to a second machine: one rotating assembly does two jobs.

Because the machine runs at turbocharger speed, its output must be conditioned through power electronics before it can be synchronised with the ship's system - the machine's frequency follows the turbocharger, which follows the engine. Whether the electrical machine is built inside the turbocharger casing or mounted externally on an extension of the shaft differs between builders, and an answer should say so rather than describe one arrangement as though it were standard.

blocks.h: 7. How it works in both directions

ul: Generator mode - at high load. Where the turbine develops more power than the compressor needs, the electrical machine absorbs the surplus and delivers power to the ship. It is doing the same thermodynamic job as a power turbine generator, but without a second turbine, a bypass or a gearbox.
Motor mode - at low load and in transients. Where the exhaust cannot spin the turbocharger fast enough, the same machine drives the compressor, restoring scavenge pressure independently of the gas.

Control. The decision between the two is continuous and automatic, following engine load and the demanded rate of change. In effect the turbocharger's speed is no longer a passive consequence of exhaust energy but a controlled variable.

blocks.h: 8. What it buys, and what it costs

rows: It spans the whole load range in one installation - harvesting at the top and supporting at the bottom. This is its principal argument against the other two devices

The electrical machine lives in a hostile place - very high rotational speed, high temperature, and the vibration and contamination of the turbocharger environment. Bearings, cooling and insulation are all more demanding
Compact - no second turbine casing, no bypass line, no reduction gearing, and a smaller demand on machinery space
Power electronics are essential, and they bring their own environmental limits, cooling requirements and failure modes
Improved transient response and load acceptance, because compressor speed can be raised on demand rather than waiting for the gas
The generating benefit is still bounded by surplus energy, so at low load it can only motor, not generate
Reduced dependence on auxiliary blowers and better low-load combustion
Overhaul and inspection now involve an electrical machine integrated with a component that is routinely opened for cleaning and balancing

blocks.h: (c) Electro-assist turbochargers (5 marks)
9. What it is

blocks.p: An electro-assist turbocharger carries an electric motor on the turbocharger shaft whose function is to drive the compressor when the exhaust gas cannot. It is characterised by motoring rather than generating: it consumes electrical power from the ship in order to improve the engine's air supply, and the return is combustion quality and responsiveness rather than direct electrical output.

The terms 'hybrid' and 'electro-assist' overlap in industry usage and many real machines can both motor and generate. The distinction used here - hybrid characterised by its generating capability, electro-assist by its motoring capability - is the one that makes the stem's three-way division intelligible, and the categories are not watertight.

blocks.h: 10. The problem it solves

blocks.p: A turbocharger is a self-regulating machine and that is normally a virtue: more fuel means more exhaust energy means more air. But the same feedback works against the engine at the bottom of the range and during changes of load.

ul: At low load - and a ship deliberately slow-steaming spends most of her life there - the exhaust has too little energy. The turbocharger runs slowly, scavenge air pressure falls, the air-fuel ratio deteriorates, combustion is incomplete, the engine smokes, deposits build in the gas ways and the exhaust boiler, and thermal loading becomes uneven.
During acceleration and load acceptance the engine needs air before it has produced the exhaust energy to supply it. The turbocharger lags, and the interval is filled with poor combustion.

The traditional answer is the auxiliary blower - electrically driven fans that cut in below a set scavenge pressure. They work, but they are essentially an on-off assist at the very bottom of the range.

blocks.p: The electro-assist motor does the same job continuously, proportionally and over a much wider load range, by acting on the turbocharger itself rather than by blowing air past it.

blocks.h: 11. What it buys, and what it costs

rows: Clean, stable running at low load - better air-fuel ratio, less smoke, less fouling of gas ways, economiser and turbine, and more even thermal loading
It consumes electrical power. The gain is in combustion quality and in avoided fouling and maintenance, not in generated output, and an honest answer says so
Faster load acceptance and better manoeuvring behaviour, because compressor speed can be commanded rather than waited for
It adds an electrical machine and power electronics to the turbocharger, with the same environmental and maintenance consequences as the hybrid
It supports the operating profile the industry has adopted - slow steaming and derated engines - which is precisely why it counts as a current development rather than a curiosity
Benefit is concentrated at the bottom of the range, so a ship that trades at sustained high output gains little
It reduces dependence on auxiliary blowers and the wear and noise associated with them
Any change to a certified engine's arrangement engages the NOx Technical File and the ship's certification, and must be handled accordingly

blocks.h: 12. Choosing between them

blocks.p: The three are not competitors on a single scale, and the right way to close a short-notes answer is to say what determines the choice.

ul: A ship on long ocean passages at sustained high output has a large, continuously available surplus and little low-load problem. The power turbine generator suits her, and its bulk and cost are justified by the hours it will run.
A ship that slow-steams, manoeuvres frequently, or whose engine has been derated has the opposite problem: little surplus and a chronic air deficit. Electro-assist is the device that helps her.

A ship whose profile is genuinely mixed - and most are - has a case for the hybrid, which addresses both ends in one compact installation at the price of putting an electrical machine in the most demanding location on the engine.

The determining factor is therefore the operating profile, not the technology. A device fitted to the wrong profile returns nothing, and that judgement is what a Chief Engineer brings to the question.

blocks.h: 13. What these developments mean for the operating engineer

ol: Exhaust-side cleanliness now has a direct financial value. Fouling of the turbine, nozzle ring and gas ways has always cost scavenge pressure; where energy is being harvested it now costs recovered electrical power as well. Turbine washing, inspection intervals and - the connection to fuel quality on this same paper - the combustion behaviour of the fuel being burned all bear directly on the return.

New failure modes. Bypass valves and their actuators; gearing and its lubrication; high-speed electrical machines with their own bearing, cooling and insulation requirements; and power electronics, which are the least tolerant component of the whole arrangement to heat, humidity and vibration.

The electrical plant becomes more complex. A generator whose speed follows engine load requires conditioning and careful synchronisation, and - more importantly - it disappears when the main engine load falls. Blackout prevention, load shedding, standby start and changeover philosophy must all account for that, and the arrangement engages the requirements governing the ship's main source of electrical power.
Certification. Any alteration to the certified engine arrangement engages the NOx Technical File and the ship's certification, and cannot be treated as a purely technical retrofit.

Operating discipline. Where a device is engaged only above a threshold load, the engineer must understand the engagement logic well enough to recognise when the machine is not contributing and why - and, in the case of a power turbine, to treat a bypass valve defect as an engine air-supply problem first and a lost-generation problem second.

blocks.h: 14. Where this fits in the wider picture

blocks.p: Set these three developments against the two other efficiency routes on this paper and their place becomes clear. Hull and dimensional optimisation reduces the power the ship needs; speed reduction reduces it further and more sharply. These devices do something different: they take the energy already lost and turn part of it back into useful work, without altering the combustion process and therefore without disturbing the engine's emissions certification.

Two honest qualifications belong in the closing. The gains are incremental - none of these devices transforms a ship's efficiency the way a change of fuel or a substantial reduction in speed does. And they are load-profile dependent, so the same installation that pays handsomely on one trade returns nothing on another. What has made them worth fitting is that efficiency is now measured and increasingly priced - through the design and operational indices, and through the carbon-pricing measures under development at this sitting - so that every kilowatt recovered from the funnel has a value it did not previously have.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: The command is write short notes, which is a licence to be compact - but three definitions will not earn sixteen marks. The examiner has prefaced the question with 'referring to latest developments in turbocharger application', which means each device needs a reason for existing, not just a description. The reliable shape is the same four questions for each: what is it, how is it arranged, what does it buy, and what does it cost? Repeating that structure lets the examiner mark all three against the same headings, which is exactly what a short-notes answer should do.

Write the two-sentence premise first - the exhaust is the biggest loss, and a modern turbocharger leaves a surplus at high load. It costs almost nothing and it converts three unconnected notes into one argument. Then close with the comparison. Those two additions are the difference between a pass and a good mark on a question where the content itself is not difficult.
Marks are 6/5/5, so the power turbine generator gets a little more. That suits it, because it has the most to describe - a separate machine, a gas path, gearing and an engagement threshold.

blocks.h: The idea underneath all three

blocks.p: Turbocharging began as a way of getting more power out of a given engine: force more air in, burn more fuel, make more power from the same cylinders. Efficiency was a by-product. What has changed is that turbochargers got good enough for the arithmetic to invert. At high load a modern turbocharger's turbine can develop more power than its own compressor absorbs, and that difference is a continuously available stream of energy that used to go up the funnel.

Once you see it that way, all three devices are answers to a single question - what do we do with that difference? - and the third one is the same question asked with the sign reversed: what do we do when there isn't one? Because the same feedback loop that produces a surplus at high load produces a shortage at low load, and the industry now runs ships at low load deliberately.
That symmetry is the most useful thing to carry out of this question. High load: too much exhaust energy, so take some out. Low load: too little, so put some in. Everything else is arrangement.
