points: Document of Compliance to the Company, up to five years, annually verified
Safety Management Certificate to the ship
Interim certification, and the consequence of a major non-conformity

steps.title: The role the SMS plays in implementing the Code
points: It converts objectives into procedures that a named person performs
It creates the shore-to-ship link through the Designated Person
It generates the evidence on which compliance is verified

steps.title: Continuous improvement - the mechanism
points: Element 9 - report, investigate and analyse; corrective action to prevent recurrence
Element 12 - internal audit at intervals not exceeding twelve months
Periodic evaluation of effectiveness, and timely corrective action by those responsible

steps.title: Continuous improvement - why it is the significant part
points: Without it the SMS becomes a static manual that describes a ship nobody operates
It is what makes the system self-correcting rather than merely documented
It is the difference between a certified company and a safe one

steps.title: Why the Code exists, and the shift it represents
points: A major ro-ro passenger casualty and an inquiry that found the fault ashore, not only aboard
The move from regulating hardware to regulating management
From compliance by inspection to compliance by demonstrated system

steps.title: Evolution one - from recommendation to mandatory instrument
points: Adopted as an Assembly resolution, A.741(18)
Made mandatory through SOLAS chapter IX, phased by ship type
The single largest change in its history

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Two limbs at 8 marks each, and the command verb in both is EXAMINE, which is stronger than 'describe' - it asks for analysis, not recitation. Limb (a) has three demands: the ROLE of the SMS in IMPLEMENTING the Code, its COMPONENTS, and the SIGNIFICANCE OF CONTINUOUS IMPROVEMENT. The third is the analytical one and it is where the discriminating marks are. Limb (b) asks for the EVOLUTION of the Code in response to EMERGING CHALLENGES, and then names three: technological advancements, cyber risks, and environmental sustainability. Those three are a printed checklist and each must be addressed by name.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 8 + 8, printed. In limb (a), roughly one mark for what the Code is and how it binds, one for what an SMS is, two for the functional requirements and the Part A components, one for the certification layer, one for the role the SMS plays in implementation, and two for continuous improvement - its mechanism and its significance. In limb (b), roughly two marks for the origin and the shift from hardware to management, one for the move from recommendation to mandatory instrument, one for the amendment chain, and then four spread across the three named challenges, with cyber risk carrying the most because it is the one with a named resolution behind it.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That the candidate knows the Code operates through a SYSTEM rather than through prescriptive rules, and can explain why that matters. That the candidate can give the components - either the six functional requirements at 1.4 or the twelve Part A elements, and preferably both, showing how one maps onto the other. That the candidate treats continuous improvement as a MECHANISM with named parts - reporting and analysis under element 9, internal audit at intervals not exceeding twelve months under element 12, management review and corrective action - rather than as a slogan. And in limb (b), that the candidate can name MSC.428(98) for cyber risk, and can be honest that the Code has adapted largely by GENERALITY rather than by repeated amendment.

decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: MEDIUM - And higher than the intake's LOW. The CODE ITSELF is stable - the operative text has been in force since 1 January 2015 - so limb (a) carries little risk. LIMB (B) IS THE EXPOSURE, and it is structural rather than accidental: a limb that asks about EMERGING challenges is a limb whose correct content moves with the sitting date even though the printed words do not. The donor is twenty-two months later, which is the longest backward reach on this paper, and its limb (b) will have been written to a mid-2026 view of what was emerging. Everything after August 2024 is stripped.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW. The ISM Code applies through SOLAS chapter IX and the flag State; the DG Shipping implementation is not asked for and is not described. The Merchant Shipping Act 2025 commenced 15 March 2026 and does not appear.
technical_ambiguities: 'Components' of the SMS could mean the six FUNCTIONAL REQUIREMENTS at element 1.4 or the twelve PART A ELEMENTS. The answer gives both and shows how they relate, because the functional requirements are what the Code demands an SMS contain, and the elements are how the Code then specifies each of them. Giving only one is defensible; giving both and explaining the relationship is better and costs three lines.

'Continuous improvement' is not a defined term in the Code and does not appear as a heading. It is an outcome produced by several elements working together - reporting and analysis at 9, maintenance at 10, and verification, review and evaluation at 12 - and the answer says so rather than pretending there is a clause called continuous improvement.

'Evolution ... including technological advancements, cyber risks, and environmental sustainability' invites the claim that the Code has been repeatedly amended to address each. IT HAS NOT. The Code's text has been substantially unchanged since MSC.353(92), and it has accommodated all three largely through the GENERALITY of its existing requirements - with cyber the one exception, where MSC.428(98) directed that the risks be addressed within the existing SMS framework. The honest answer says this, and it is a stronger answer than an invented amendment history.

'Environmental sustainability' is the loosest of the three. Environmental protection has been in the Code's title and objectives since adoption, but the decarbonisation instruments - the SEEMP, EEXI, the CII - sit in MARPOL Annex VI and NOT in the ISM Code. The answer distinguishes them, because conflating them is a substantive error.
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Fourteen numbered sections under two limb headings, eight and six. Limb (a) builds from the instrument, through the definition of an SMS, the functional requirements, the twelve elements, the certification layer, the role in implementation, and closes on continuous improvement in two sections - mechanism, then significance - because that is the analytical demand. Limb (b) is chronological then thematic: origin and the shift it represents, the move to mandatory status, the amendment chain, and then the three named challenges each under its own heading so the examiner can tick them. Tables carry the functional requirements against the elements, and the certification layer.

questions.understand_first: Every rule of maritime safety written before this one told you something about the ship: how thick the steel, how many lifeboats, how the bulkheads are arranged, what the fire pumps must deliver. Inspect the ship and you could tell whether the rule had been obeyed. But ships kept being lost that satisfied every one of those requirements, and when the losses were investigated the failure was repeatedly found not in the hardware and not even entirely on board. It lay in how the operation was run: nobody had written down who was responsible for what, the people ashore were commercially motivated to press for a departure and nobody aboard felt able to refuse, a defect had been reported before and nothing had come of it, and there was no route by which a concern could travel from the engine room to a decision-maker in the office. You cannot fix that by specifying the steel. So the response was a different kind of instrument altogether - one that does not tell you what to build but requires you to run a system: write down your safety policy; write procedures for the operations that matter; say who is responsible and to whom they report; make sure a specific named person ashore has a direct line to the top of the company and cannot be filtered out; state plainly that the master may overrule anyone in the interests of safety; prepare for emergencies and practise them; and - this is the part that makes the whole thing work - report what goes wrong, investigate it, fix the cause rather than the symptom, audit yourselves regularly, and change the system when it turns out to be wrong. The company is then certified not on the condition of its ships but on whether it actually operates that system, and the ship carries a certificate saying she is operated in accordance with it. The insight worth carrying is that the last part is the point: a system that is written and never revised is just a shelf of manuals. The Code's real subject is not the procedures but the loop that keeps correcting them.
questions.memory_cue: (a) EIGHT: WHAT IT IS (1), WHAT AN SMS IS (2), SIX FUNCTIONALS (3), TWELVE ELEMENTS (4), CERTIFICATES (5), THE ROLE (6), THE LOOP - HOW (7), THE LOOP - WHY (8). (b) SIX: WHY IT EXISTS (9), BECAME MANDATORY (10), AMENDED (11), then the THREE PRINTED CHALLENGES - TECH (12), CYBER (13), ENVIRONMENT (14).

quick_revision.recall_15s: ISM Code adopted by A.741(18), mandatory through SOLAS chapter IX, amended through MSC.353(92) (adopted 21 June 2013, in force 1 January 2015). It regulates MANAGEMENT, not hardware. SMS = a structured and documented system enabling Company personnel to implement effectively the Company safety and environmental protection policy. SIX functional requirements at 1.4: a safety and environmental protection policy; instructions and procedures for safe operation and environmental protection; defined levels of authority and lines of communication; procedures for reporting accidents and non-conformities; procedures to prepare for and respond to emergencies; procedures for internal audits and management reviews. TWELVE Part A elements; Part B is certification - DOC to the Company up to five years, annually verified within three months of the anniversary date, and the SMC to the ship. CONTINUOUS IMPROVEMENT = element 9 reporting and analysis with corrective action to prevent recurrence, plus element 12 internal audits at intervals NOT EXCEEDING TWELVE MONTHS (exceptionally extendable by not more than three), periodic evaluation of effectiveness, and timely corrective action. EVOLUTION: recommendation to mandatory; the amendment chain; and adaptation to technology, CYBER (MSC.428(98), 16 June 2017, bearing in mind MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3) and environment MOSTLY BY GENERALITY rather than by amendment.
critical_numbers: ISM Code adopted by resolution A.741(18); mandatory through SOLAS chapter IX

quick_revision.critical_regulation: The ISM Code as adopted by resolution A.741(18) and amended through MSC.353(92), made mandatory by SOLAS chapter IX; together with resolution MSC.428(98) on maritime cyber risk management in safety management systems.
quick_revision.major_trap: Claiming the Code has been repeatedly amended to address technology, cyber risk and environmental sustainability. IT HAS NOT. Its text has been substantially unchanged since MSC.353(92) took effect on 1 January 2015, and it has absorbed all three largely through the GENERALITY of its existing requirements - the one instrument-level response being MSC.428(98), which directed that cyber risks be addressed WITHIN the existing SMS framework rather than by adding a new element. The second trap is putting the SEEMP, EEXI or the CII inside the ISM Code; they are MARPOL Annex VI instruments.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the SMS and ISM evolution question.
retrieval_cards.answer: (a) 1 what the Code is and how it binds. 2 what an SMS is. 3 the six functional requirements. 4 the twelve Part A elements. 5 the certification layer. 6 the role the SMS plays in implementing the Code. 7 continuous improvement - the mechanism. 8 continuous improvement - why it is significant. (b) 9 why the Code exists and the shift from hardware to management. 10 recommendation to mandatory instrument. 11 the amendment chain. 12 technological advancement. 13 cyber risk. 14 environmental sustainability and the honest limit.
retrieval_cards.why: 8 + 8, and the verb is EXAMINE in both limbs. Sections 7-8 and 12-14 are the analytical parts and they carry the discriminating marks; the printed three challenges must each get their own heading.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the six functional requirements for a Safety Management System.
retrieval_cards.answer: Element 1.4. Every company should develop, implement and maintain an SMS which includes: (1) a safety and environmental protection policy; (2) instructions and procedures to ensure safe operation of ships and protection of the environment in compliance with relevant international and flag State legislation; (3) defined levels of authority and lines of communication between, and amongst, shore and shipboard personnel; (4) procedures for reporting accidents and non-conformities with the provisions of the Code; (5) procedures to prepare for and respond to emergency situations; and (6) procedures for internal audits and management reviews.
retrieval_cards.why: The single most quotable list in the question and it maps directly onto the Part A elements. Requirement (3) is the one that answers what the Code was written to fix.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is a Safety Management System, and why does the Code work through one?
retrieval_cards.answer: A structured and documented system enabling Company personnel to implement effectively the Company safety and environmental protection policy. The Code works through it because safety of operation cannot be prescribed the way scantlings or lifeboat capacity can - the right procedure depends on the ship, the trade, the crew and the company. So the Code sets OBJECTIVES (safety at sea, prevention of human injury or loss of life, avoidance of damage to the environment and to property) and REQUIRES A SYSTEM that delivers them, leaving the company to write procedures suited to its own operation and then holding it to what it wrote.
retrieval_cards.why: The conceptual heart of limb (a). It explains why the Code says 'should establish procedures' rather than telling you what the procedures are.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the twelve Part A elements.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 General (definitions, objectives, application, functional requirements). 2 Safety and Environmental Protection Policy. 3 Company Responsibilities and Authority. 4 Designated Person(s). 5 Master's Responsibility and Authority. 6 Resources and Personnel. 7 Shipboard Operations. 8 Emergency Preparedness. 9 Reports and Analysis of Non-conformities, Accidents and Hazardous Occurrences. 10 Maintenance of the Ship and Equipment. 11 Documentation. 12 Company Verification, Review and Evaluation. Part B then adds 13 Certification and Periodical Verification, 14 Interim Certification, 15 Verification and 16 Forms of Certificates.
retrieval_cards.why: 'Components' in the printed stem. Give these and the six functional requirements and the components demand is fully answered.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does the Code actually produce continuous improvement?
retrieval_cards.answer: Through three elements working together. ELEMENT 9 - the SMS must include procedures ensuring that non-conformities, accidents and hazardous situations are REPORTED to the Company, INVESTIGATED and ANALYSED with the object of improving safety and pollution prevention, and the Company must establish procedures for implementing CORRECTIVE ACTION INCLUDING MEASURES INTENDED TO PREVENT RECURRENCE. ELEMENT 12 - internal safety audits on board and ashore at intervals NOT EXCEEDING TWELVE MONTHS, exceptionally extendable by not more than three; periodic verification that those undertaking delegated ISM tasks conform; PERIODIC EVALUATION OF THE EFFECTIVENESS of the SMS; auditors independent of the areas audited where practicable; results brought to the attention of all personnel responsible; and TIMELY CORRECTIVE ACTION by the management personnel responsible. ELEMENT 10 supplies the maintenance and critical-equipment feedback that populates the loop.
retrieval_cards.why: 'Significance of continuous improvement' is worth two marks and cannot be earned by asserting that improvement is important. Name the mechanism.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How did the ISM Code respond to cyber risk?
retrieval_cards.answer: By resolution MSC.428(98), MARITIME CYBER RISK MANAGEMENT IN SAFETY MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS, adopted 16 June 2017. It recognised the urgent need to raise awareness of cyber risk threats and vulnerabilities to support safe and secure shipping that is operationally resilient to cyber risks, and bore in mind MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3, the Guidelines on maritime cyber risk management approved by the Facilitation Committee at its forty-first session and by the MSC at its ninety-eighth session. CRUCIALLY, NO NEW ELEMENT WAS ADDED TO THE CODE. The response was to direct that cyber risks be addressed within the EXISTING safety management system - using the Code's own risk assessment, procedures, familiarisation and audit machinery.
retrieval_cards.why: The best single illustration of how the Code evolves: not by growing, but by having been written generally enough that a threat nobody imagined in 1993 fits inside it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Has the ISM Code been amended to deal with environmental sustainability and decarbonisation?
retrieval_cards.answer: NO, and saying so is the stronger answer. Environmental protection has been in the Code's TITLE and in its objectives since adoption - the objectives include avoidance of damage to the environment, and the policy required by element 2 is a safety AND ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION policy - so the Code has always had an environmental limb. But the decarbonisation instruments are NOT in the ISM Code: the SEEMP, EEXI and the CII rating are MARPOL Annex VI measures. What the ISM Code contributes is the management framework through which those obligations are implemented on board - procedures, responsibilities, records, audit and review - which is a real contribution and a different one.
retrieval_cards.why: The commonest substantive error on limb (b), and correcting it demonstrates that you know which instrument does what.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why was the ISM Code needed when SOLAS already existed?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because SOLAS regulates the SHIP and the failures were in the MANAGEMENT. Investigations into major casualties repeatedly found ships that complied with the construction and equipment requirements and were lost anyway, because responsibilities ashore were undefined, commercial pressure reached the master unopposed, defects had been reported before without action, and there was no route by which a concern could reach a decision-maker. None of that is curable by a construction standard. The ISM Code therefore regulates the SYSTEM: defined authority and lines of communication, a Designated Person with direct access to the highest level of management, the master's overriding authority expressly stated, reporting and analysis of non-conformities, and audit. It shifted compliance from what can be inspected on a ship to what can be demonstrated about a company.
retrieval_cards.why: The opening of limb (b) and the point on which the whole evolution argument rests.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The ISM Code as amended through MSC.353(92) is the operative text at this sitting, and no later amendment is asserted.
reverify_before_publication.why: Stated as a limitation of the held chain rather than as a positive finding. The corpus holds A.741(18), MSC.104(73), MSC.179(79), MSC.195(80), MSC.273(85) and MSC.353(92) as official resolutions; MSC.353(92) was read at source and is dated 21 June 2013 with entry into force 1 January 2015. A copy that predates a later amendment cannot prove one does not exist, so the answer asserts none in either direction.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The wording and element structure of the ISM Code quoted in this answer.
reverify_before_publication.why: THE CORPUS ISM HOLDING IS A TRANSCRIPTION IN DOCX FORM, NOT AN IMO-PUBLISHED PDF OF THE CONSOLIDATED CODE. It was read in full this session and its content is consistent with the amendment chain held as official resolutions, but a reviewer should treat the element wording as a transcription rather than as a certified consolidation and may wish to spot-check the intervals at 12.1 and 13.4 against a published edition.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The treatment of MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3 and of resolution A.1118(30).
reverify_before_publication.why: MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3 is identified from the recitals of MSC.428(98), which were read at source. MIW HOLDS NO COPY OF THE CIRCULAR IN ANY REVISION, so NO REVISION NUMBER, DATE OR CONTENT is asserted - the Guidelines have been revised more than once and any revision stated would be a currency exposure. A.1118(30) is identified by subject matter only and was not read at source.
